Description: Exposed by CAVEAT-412 once readiness stopped accepting 'switched on' as evidence. input/bldg1_timetable.csv is 55 KB and feeds.yaml declares synthetic_timetable enabled: true with the note that rows 'land in the events store via the T25 institutional adapter' - the events table holds 51,456 rows across anomaly, booking, access, workorder and asset_outage, and NOT ONE timetable or session row. weather_external's rest_poll feed likewise registers no points in the graph. Related: NOTE-407, where the feed framework's own auto-registered point declares a storage location that does not exist - the same subsystem failing the same way.
Root_Cause: Unknown. The feed registry loads and reports its feeds; whether the timetable adapter runs, fails silently, or was never wired to the events writer has not been traced.
Fix_Approach: Trace one feed end to end: does FeedRegistry tick it, does the adapter parse the CSV, and does anything write the result. Worth doing with NOTE-407 in the same pass, since both are the feed framework not completing the connect-data half of contract 8. Until then a timetable question correctly declines rather than answering wrongly, which is why this is P2 and not P1.
Verification: The timetable no longer depends on the feed that never fired. input/bldg1_timetable.csv is now lifted as a record register: 675 sessions across 44 rooms, every room named by the label the graph carries. ontosage:TimetabledSession went from 0 instances to 675. Live: "Which teaching sessions are scheduled in Room 1.06?" returns the 23 sessions in that room. The weather feed remains empty and is tracked separately.

Title: The deliberation fetch pulls ~2.7M rows per question, and my own cadence change made the limit wrong
Description: Measured while resuming the stakeholder capture on the local model: a deliberative question logs '[fetch] 1859 series from 10 tables (window=72.0h, per-uuid limit=1440)' with single table queries returning 322,560 rows (224 uuids x 1440). Across ten tables that is roughly 2.7M rows for ONE question. Local median is 17.6s/question against the hosted 7.7s, and the slowest questions hit WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_S=120 outright - 1 of the first 17 local rows timed out, so those questions yield no measurement at all.
Root_Cause: TWO causes, and the second is mine. (1) The backfill gave every sensor real history, so a limit that used to return little now returns its full quota. (2) _PER_UUID_LIMIT is DERIVED as stuck's 6h at _FASTEST_CADENCE_S = 30.0 seconds - and CAVEAT-405 has just changed the cadences: the fastest is now 60s (co2/occupancy/noise), with most modalities at 300s. Six hours at 60s is 360 samples, not 720, so the derived 1440 is roughly double what any detector now needs. CAVEAT-401's own note says to re-check this whenever the cadence or a detector threshold changes. The cadence changed and I did not re-check - the same coupling, one turn later.
Fix_Approach: Re-derive _FASTEST_CADENCE_S from sensor_signal.CADENCE_S rather than restating 30.0, so the two cannot drift again, and let the fetch bound itself by TIME rather than by sample count where the adapter allows it. NOT CHANGED NOW, deliberately: the capture is running and altering the system mid-measurement is what CAVEAT-173 and BUG-176 are about. The timeouts are a real property of the system as it stands and belong in this baseline.
Verification: VERIFIED BY RE-MEASUREMENT. _FASTEST_CADENCE_S is now READ from the publisher's own CADENCE_S map rather than restated as 30.0, so the derived _PER_UUID_LIMIT fell from 1440 to 720 - still 12 hours of history against stuck's 6-hour requirement, at half the rows fetched. Re-running the 82 timed-out questions with the fix deployed: 82 timeouts -> 7, a 91% reduction, and the capture is now 2,473 OK of 2,480. Local median fell to 9.0s with p90 44.6s. 6 tests pin the coupling so a cadence change cannot silently oversize the fetch again - which is exactly how this arose, one turn after CAVEAT-405 changed every cadence.

Title: 62 failures in six hours logged an empty message, hiding an 11% silent quality degradation
Description: Measured on bldg1 during the stakeholder capture: 62 WARNING lines whose message is empty - the line ends in a colon and says nothing. 52 of them are '[capability_graph] amenity fetch failed, deferring to KB:', 6 'GraphDB retrieval failed:', 2 '[inventory] class census failed:', 2 '[anomaly-scan] sweep failed (will retry):'. The capability count is the serious one: 52 against 488 capability questions in that run is roughly 11% of capability answers ABANDONING THE ONTOLOGY and falling back to the document KB - a contract-2 (TTL-first) bypass with no record of why.
Root_Cause: Two causes stacked. (1) The handlers log f'...: {e}', and several exception classes render as an empty string - httpx.ReadTimeout, httpx.ConnectTimeout, asyncio.TimeoutError, a bare Exception. (2) The thing being hidden: _default_sparql_exec uses timeout=15.0 and GraphDB exceeds it under concurrent load - the observed gap was exactly 15s (21:22:50 -> 21:23:05). The load is the hourly anomaly sweep, which takes 598 SECONDS per pass (CAVEAT-414) and overlaps whatever else is running. The FALLBACK IS CORRECT BEHAVIOUR - degrade rather than fail - and its invisibility is not.
Fix_Approach: Never log a bare exception. shared.utils.describe_exception() always names the class, which is usually the whole diagnosis, and the four measured sites now use it; the anomaly sweep also logs exc_info because a retrying background loop is the hardest kind to diagnose. NOT YET ADDRESSED, and the more important half: the 15s SPARQL timeout against a sweep that monopolises GraphDB for ten minutes an hour. Raising the timeout trades one failure mode for slower turns; the real fix is CAVEAT-414. Source edited, NOT deployed - the orchestrator must not be restarted mid-capture.
Verification: V12-19 2026-09-12: closed at the LOGGER, not at the 871 call sites. shared.utils.get_logger() now attaches a filter that rewrites any WARNING-or-above whose FORMATTED message is empty or ends in a colon, appending '<NO DETAIL -- the exception carried no message. Wrap it in describe_exception() to record its class.>'. It cannot recover the class (that information is gone by the time the string exists) but it makes the emptiness VISIBLE, which is the difference between a log nobody can act on and one that says where to look. DEBUG is left alone. Verified on the exact measured shape: '[capability_graph] amenity fetch failed, deferring to KB: ' with asyncio.TimeoutError and a bare Exception(). LIVE RE-ASK OWED: re-run a capability-heavy capture and confirm zero empty warnings and that the 52 capability deferrals now name their cause. || 13 tests. One of them caught a defect in the fix itself: describe_exception called str(exc), which a custom __str__ can raise - a function whose whole job is describing a failure becoming a second failure inside an except block, where it would mask the original entirely. Now returns '(unprintable)' instead. The empty-message count is expected to fall to zero after the next orchestrator restart; the 52 fallbacks themselves will not fall until CAVEAT-414 is fixed.

Title: The Source label 'stakeholder_catalogue_37' covers 31 of the 37 catalogues
Description: QuestionBank/Talking_Abacws_37_Stakeholder_Catalogues/ holds 37 PDFs. tasks/smart_building_questions.csv Source='stakeholder_catalogue_37' holds 2,480 questions across exactly 31 distinct Stakeholder_Role labels at 80 each. Six catalogues were never extracted, worth roughly 480 questions: Academic office occupants, Lecturers and tutors, PhD students, Research staff, Taught postgraduate students, Undergraduate students.
Root_Cause: MY FINDING WAS WRONG AND I CHECKED IT BEFORE ACTING. I reported six catalogues as never extracted. They are all in the bank: 480 rows with IDs UG-/PGT-/PHD-/RS-/LT-/AO- under Source='supervisor_catalogue_2026-08', with role labels in the SINGULAR ('Undergraduate Student') where the PDF filenames are plural ('Undergraduate students'). My name normalisation stripped punctuation but not the trailing 's', so six exact matches read as six absences. 2,480 + 480 = 2,960 = 37 x 80: every catalogue is present, and the occupant half is already inside the 1,580-question golden baseline, so it has been measured for longer than the other 31 have.
Fix_Approach: What remains is a LABELLING caveat, not a data gap: a reader filtering on Source='stakeholder_catalogue_37' gets 31 of the 37 catalogues and nothing says so, which is how I misread it. Either relabel those 480 rows to the catalogue source they came from, or rename the source so it stops implying 37. Do not re-extract anything - that would duplicate 480 questions.
Verification: Verified by ID prefix rather than by role name: the six prefixes the extractor's own docstring names ('Six were already in smart_building_questions.csv, 480 rows, IDs UG-/PGT-/PHD-/RS-/LT-/AO-') return exactly 480 rows across exactly those six roles. The docstring said so all along; I matched on filenames instead of reading it. Coverage claims over the 2,480 are still 'operational roles only' - that part of the original note stands - but the occupant questions are measured elsewhere.

Title: A Python tuple decided which record classes the building could be asked about
Description: record_registry._RECORD_CLASSES was a hardcoded list of twelve class names, and record_classes() only ever looked for those. Adding ontosage:CleaningTask, ontosage:PublicEvent and ontosage:AccessPermission to the TBox with lay terms, plus documents lifted into 62 instances, changed NOTHING: every question about them still reached the document lane and was told the building holds no such record. Discovery from the ontology returns 22 classes against the hardcoded 12, so TEN classes the ontology already declared were unreachable - AccessEvent, AlarmEvent, AnomalyEvent, AssetStatus, ClosurePeriod, ServiceSchedule among them.
Root_Cause: A contract-2 violation with teeth. 'TTL before YAML' and 'extend the TTL before adding code' are the design rules, and this made the code the gate: the ontology could declare a class, the lifter could populate it, the router could have lay terms for it, and a tuple in Python still decided it did not exist. Nothing failed loudly - the lane declined honestly, which reads like an absent register rather than a wiring gap.
Fix_Approach: Discover the classes by querying for everything beneath ontosage:Record and ontosage:IntervalRecord, keeping the old tuple as a FALLBACK so a GraphDB hiccup degrades to the classes that existed rather than to none.
Verification: Verified live on four questions that had all declined or quoted before, now all COMPUTED through the metadata/SPARQL lane: 'my cleaning zone and task list for this shift' -> '13 tasks scheduled, none newly added or handed over'; 'are visitors admitted and when does check-in open' -> admission, 17:30 check-in, entrance and companion policy; 'which permission groups control the Level 2 entrance and what overrides them' -> a computed table naming APG-004 and both global modes; 'which cleaning tasks are suspended' -> '2 of 30' with reasons. Found while building the first registers from a measured gap rather than from a guess.

Title: The heuristic grader marks computed answers as honest declines when they carry hedging language
Description: Re-measuring four roles after the register work reported 12 regressions. Reading all 12 leaves at most 6. FOUR are the grader misreading a good answer: AC-031 cites APG-015 and its EXTENDED time profile; CT-073 opens 'Cleaning-defect overview (30 records total)'; CT-042 and VE-004 both cite register records across 2,000+ characters. All four compute over data that did not exist yesterday and all four were graded 'honest-capability-answer' because _heuristic_grade tests for capability phrases before it tests for computation.
Root_Cause: corpus_replay._heuristic_grade orders its checks: hard failures, then quoted passage, then capability phrases ('requires', 'not currently available'), then digits. An answer that computes AND explains a caveat matches the capability branch first. The ordering was right when capability answers were mostly declines; it is wrong now that computed answers routinely carry a qualifying sentence.
Fix_Approach: Test for computation BEFORE hedging language: an answer citing a record id or a counted total is computed whatever else it says. Do NOT simply reorder - that risks the reverse error, marking a decline that mentions a number as computed, which is the failure BUG-370 and BUG-191 were both about. Needs a labelled set to sweep against, the way BUG-218's fix was measured and rejected. UNTIL THEN, the computed share is UNDERSTATED, not overstated - which is the safer direction and means the +32 point improvement is a floor rather than a ceiling. || FIXED BY NARROWING THE EVIDENCE, NOT BY REORDERING. Measured first: of 883 answers graded honest-capability-answer, 61 carried a record count or a data marker, and 56 of those 61 were pulled out by the single word 'requires'. That word is ordinary English -- 'because each task requires a different access method' is a sentence ABOUT the data, not an admission it is missing. Bare 'requires' and bare 'capability' are gone; the phrases that genuinely mean a missing capability all say WHAT is missing, so they are listed in that form ('requires sensors', 'requires hardware', 'requires integration'). Reordering was considered and REJECTED and a test pins the order: promoting the computed check above the capability check would make a decline that mentions a number read as computed, which is BUG-370 and BUG-191 exactly.
Verification: Swept over all 2,945 answered questions before and after. 57 moved honest -> computed, of which FIFTY came from the metadata lane (SPARQL over the registers) and exactly ONE was a false promotion -- a general-knowledge answer about planning law that trips the pre-existing has_counted_records heuristic. 3 moved honest -> failed, two of them arguably correct declines. So roughly 96% precision on the change, in the direction of recognising work already done. Whole corpus: computed 42.4% -> 44.3%, 1,254 -> 1,311 questions; honest declines 29.8% -> 27.8%. Every figure reported before today was therefore a FLOOR. 7 tests, and they use answers captured from the real capture rather than invented ones -- a first version failed for its own fixtures' reasons, spelling a count as 'seven' so no digit signal fired and inventing a 'quoted passage' that does not match the opener _QUOTED_PASSAGE looks for. RESIDUAL: has_counted_records still promotes a general-knowledge answer containing any 'N word' pattern. Pre-existing, 1 in 57 here, and worth its own labelled sweep before touching.

Title: The referent gate reads a descriptive phrase as a place name and declines
Description: Measured across 320 answers: 3 declines of the form 'I couldn't find X in the model', where X is 'verified corridor', 'busy corridor' and 'lift lobby'. The first two are adjective-plus-generic-noun descriptions lifted out of the question ('do the verified corridor widths on my route fit...'), not places anyone named. 0.9% of answers, and two of the three cost an answer the accessible-route register could now give.
Root_Cause: detect_typed_referent extracts a noun phrase adjacent to a space-like head word and treats it as a referent. A qualifier before a generic noun is not a name.
Fix_Approach: Tighten with care and only against a labelled set. This gate is the guard that stopped BUG-189, where a room's reading was attributed to a corridor the building does not have, so loosening it to win three answers would trade a fabrication guard for coverage - the wrong trade at any ratio. A safer route: when the gate rejects a phrase but a record register can answer the question, decline WITH what the register holds rather than with the bare 'not found'. || RESOLVED DIFFERENTLY 2026-09-05. Investigating the decline exposed a larger defect in the same sentence: _suggest_terms matched any entity whose NAME contains the word and never asked what kind of thing was missing, although TypedReferent.kind was sitting in the caller. Live: "verified corridor" suggested CCTV cameras, "lift lobby" suggested patrol checkpoints, "room" suggested gas sensors - each offered under "What this building does have", in place of the space asked for. Suggestions are now constrained to the referent's own Brick root. The gate itself was NOT loosened, so the BUG-189 trade was never taken.
Verification: Live: "is chiller 7 running?" now suggests "Chiller 1" and "PUMP-CH1" (was any entity named after a chiller); a room miss suggests real room ids. The corridor and lobby cases now return NO suggestion, which is the honest answer - this building has no corridor or lobby modelled as a space, and the cameras it was offering were never an alternative. HONEST RESIDUAL: a FLOOR referent still draws fire exits whose labels carry "Floor 1 North"; they are at least Locations, and narrowing further needs a floor-specific class test that is not done. 6 tests.

Title: Writing any file under input/ while a building is parked nests the whole building on the next unpark
Description: The committed state has NO input/ directory (Workflow rule 8). I wrote input/documents/approval_evidence_register.md while bldg1 was parked; the Write tool created the parent directories, so input/ existed. The next unpark, 'mv bldg1 input', then moved the building INTO that directory instead of renaming to it, producing input/bldg1/documents/ - a double nesting. Everything still worked, because shared/building_paths.py resolves nested before flat, which is exactly why it was not obvious: 28 documents were found and indexed from the nested path while the new file sat alone in the flat one and was never read.
Root_Cause: `mv A B` renames when B does not exist and moves INTO B when it does. The park/unpark procedure relies on the first behaviour and nothing checks for the second. The nested-then-flat resolution order then hides the result rather than failing on it.
Fix_Approach: Two things. (1) Never write under input/ while parked - write to the parked folder (bldg<N>/) instead, or unpark first. (2) The unpark step in CLAUDE.md should assert that input/ does NOT exist before the mv, since that is the whole precondition and it is currently implicit. Symptom to watch for: the document indexer logging paths prefixed 'bldg1/' rather than bare filenames.
Verification: Layout flattened by hand: the stray flat document moved into the real documents directory, input/documents removed, input/bldg1/* lifted back up, input/bldg1 removed. Verified after a full reboot - input/building.yaml and input/env.building are back at the top level, 29 documents in input/documents, and approval_evidence_register.md lifted 32 records for the first time.

Title: The building named itself after a waste bin
Description: sparql_agent's building-name formatter triggered on 'building' in uq and 'name' in uq -- both SUBSTRING tests -- and then returned bindings[0]'s label whatever the query was about. Measured live while verifying the waste register: 'Where do waste stream NAMES and labels conflict within a station?' answered 'The building name is: **Reception mixed recycling**'. It named a waste bin as the building.
Root_Cause: Two defects compounding. (1) 'name' in uq matches the word 'names', so any question using the plural qualified. (2) The template read the first binding with no check that it was a building at all, so once triggered it would name the building after the first row of ANY result set. It went unnoticed because the trigger needs both words and no earlier question used them together -- the waste register created the first one.
Fix_Approach: Whole-word tests instead of substrings, and require exactly ONE binding: a building-name answer is one row by definition, while a multi-row result is a different question that happens to share two words. The word test alone is not sufficient and the test says so - 'list the names of every sensor in the building' passes the words and is stopped by the row count.
Verification: Verified live both ways: the waste question now computes '6 of 24 stations have a mismatch between the recorded stream and the label' (correct -- six rows differ, of which two are materially misleading), and 'what is the name of this building?' still answers 'Abacws Building'. 6 tests. A confident false statement about the building's own identity is the worst shape of wrong answer this system can produce and is exactly what contract 4 forbids: worse than a decline, because nothing signals it is wrong.

Title: Every register note is stored under a relative IRI and is unreachable
Description: record_documents._expand knew the prefixes ontosage: and xsd: only, while the mappings also declare rdfs:. A column declaring predicate: rdfs:comment was therefore serialised as <rdfs:comment>, a RELATIVE IRI, which GraphDB stored verbatim. Measured live on bldg1: rdfs:comment proper = 0 against 63 junk, and rdfs:label 206 junk (labels survived only because the lifter emits a proper label separately from label_column). Nothing errored: the upload succeeded and the triple counts looked correct.
Root_Cause: A prefix table that knew two of the three prefixes its own mappings use. The predicate was written as <{predicate}> without expansion, and a relative IRI is accepted by RDF rather than rejected.
Fix_Approach: One prefix table (expand_predicate) now serves both the lifter and the serialiser, so adding a prefix cannot leave the other behind. Guarded by tests/test_register_predicates_are_real_iris.py, which asserts on result.triples rather than only on the serialised text. The junk triples already in GraphDB are removed on the next re-lift plus an explicit DELETE.
Verification: Live on bldg1 after re-lift: proper rdfs:comment 0 -> 83, junk relative-IRI predicates 206+63 -> 0. 5 unit tests.

Title: Delete the 269 junk relative-IRI triples already in bldg1 GraphDB
Description: BUG-422 left 206 <rdfs:label> and 63 <rdfs:comment> triples in the live graph. The fix stops new ones; these need an explicit DELETE.
Root_Cause: Pre-existing data written before the fix.
Fix_Approach: DELETE WHERE { ?s <rdfs:label> ?o } and the same for <rdfs:comment>, then re-lift the registers so the proper comments appear.
Verification: DELETE WHERE on both junk predicates, then scripts/relift_registers.py --apply rewrote all 22 registers (343 records). Junk count now 0.

Title: Three registers named rooms the building does not have, under those names
Description: A new guard comparing every register's room-naming columns against the building's own rdfs:label values found six wrong references across two registers. event_activity called Room 1.09 a 'Quiet Room' and asserted in its closing summary that it 'is the confirmed public waiting space' - the building calls 1.09 a Computer Laboratory. waste_collection sited a sharps bin in 'Room 3.06 - Research Laboratory'; 3.06 is a Computer Laboratory. Both registers placed records in 'Room 5.04 - Academic Office'; 5.04 is a Research Laboratory.
Root_Cause: The referent-existence gate stops the MODEL inventing a place; it cannot stop a REGISTER doing it. A lifted record is graph data, so an invented room reads as an authoritative triple and an answer built on it passes every honesty check the pipeline has. Same failure as BUG-189 arriving from the data side.
Fix_Approach: Each reference repointed to a real room that fits the purpose (1.09 quiet room -> 1.25 Conference/Seminar; 5.04 office -> 5.07 Academic Office; 3.06 research lab -> 3.01 Research Laboratory). Guarded by tests/test_registers_name_rooms_the_building_has.py, which is offline and runs against the building TTL so the failure is caught before a register is ever lifted.
Verification: 34 tests pass across every register in the checkout; all 28 workspace rooms verified against the live graph too

Title: Multi-intent decomposition discards the held-record routing decision
Description: dialogue_agent resolves a question naming a record class the building HOLDS straight to metadata, skipping the LLM intent call (V7-T21 added this so lifting a register changes what can be answered). Multi-intent decomposition then ran on the result and overwrote it. Measured live: 'Who is my contact for a fault with the network, and what is their response target?' logged '[ttl-route] metadata via held record class: Department (20 instances)' immediately followed by '[multi-intent] Decomposed into 2 sub-intents: [capability, capability]'. Both clauses were answered from prose and the answer named the wrong contacts, while one department row held both the contact route and the response target.
Root_Cause: Two correct stages in the wrong order. Decomposition was gated only on a set of conversational intents and had no way to know the intent had been resolved from graph data rather than guessed.
Fix_Approach: The decomposition branch now re-checks held_record_class first and skips decomposing when the building holds a class that answers the question. A compound question is where a register is MOST useful - one SPARQL returns every column, two capability probes return two partial prose answers. The check is wrapped and defaults to False, so a graph hiccup degrades to the previous behaviour rather than breaking routing on every turn.
Verification: Live on bldg1: the network-contact question now returns DEP-07, the Network Infrastructure Lead, the 8-hour target and the escalation, all from the register. 4 unit tests in tests/test_registers_survive_multi_intent.py.

Title: A generated building TTL crash-looped the orchestrator for fifteen minutes
Description: scripts/generate_sensor_metrology.py wrote input/bldg1_sensor_metrology.ttl with full IRIs in angle brackets and declared only ontosage: and xsd:. assert_ttl_validation_or_die hard-fails startup when a per-building TTL omits @prefix bldg:, so the container restarted eight times and the stack was down for roughly fifteen minutes. A second, quieter defect in the same script derived the namespace as http://abacwsbuilding.cardiff.ac.uk/ instead of .../abacws# by preferring the shorter of the '#' and '/' splits; that file parses cleanly and would have attached 11,243 triples to subjects the graph does not have.
Root_Cause: The validator is correct and fires at BOOT, which means the first evidence of a malformed generated TTL is a container that will not start. Nothing checked the file at the point it was written.
Fix_Approach: Generator now derives the namespace with '#' taking precedence (a fragment separator terminates a namespace by definition) and emits bldg: prefixed terms. tests/test_building_ttl_declares_the_bldg_prefix.py checks every per-building TTL offline, mirroring the validator's own schema and scaffolding exclusions, and asserts that one building declares exactly one namespace. Its first draft globbed bldg* and failed on four files in bldg2_source/, a staging folder nothing loads - scoped to folders holding a building.yaml.
Verification: Live: 2,728 sensors carry samplingIntervalS and archivalIntervalS, 1,929 carry calibratedOn/DueOn/Method, 194 overdue. 161 tests pass across all four buildings.

Title: A reporting interval is inferred from row spacing instead of read from the declaration
Description: After 2,728 sensors were given an explicit ontosage:samplingIntervalS, 'How often does a CO2 sensor report?' answered 'every 30 seconds'. The declared interval for CO2 is 60, and the publisher's own CADENCE_S map says 60. The answer was derived from the spacing of the rows it happened to fetch rather than from the building's declaration of its own instrument. Separately, 'How many sensors are overdue for calibration?' returned an empty intent and no answer at all, so the 194 overdue calibrations now in the graph are unreachable by that phrasing.
Root_Cause: The metrology triples attach to sensors rather than to a Record subclass, so held_record_class does not claim them, and no lane reads samplingIntervalS. A figure computed from sampled rows will differ from the declared cadence whenever the fetch window or the publisher jitters.
Fix_Approach: Two parts, neither done. (1) Read the declared interval when one exists and only fall back to inference when it does not, saying which was used. (2) Give the metrology a route: either a record class over sensor metrology or a concept-resolver mapping for calibration vocabulary. Sized before doing: the immediate purpose of the metrology was to populate the completeness and calibration gate inputs, which it does.
Verification: Live on bldg1, all three original failures corrected. "When was the CO2 sensor in Room 5.01 last calibrated?" -> "last calibrated on November 17, 2025, two-point span check against a certified gas, next due November 16, 2026" (was "no calibration record found"). "How often does a CO2 sensor report?" -> "every 60 seconds", the declared value (was "30 seconds", inferred from row spacing). "How many sensors are overdue for calibration?" -> "194" with the 2,728/1,929 context (was the building census). REQUIRED GUARDS IN FIVE INDEPENDENT COMPONENTS, each of which claimed the question in turn and produced a different wrong answer: the document-KB probe in dialogue_agent, the routing contract parse stage, the routing contract post stage, the capability metrics path, and is_inventory_count_question - plus is_inventory_question on a neighbouring shape. An unscoped metrology question is COUNTED in the graph rather than listed under a LIMIT and counted by the model. 22 unit tests pin all five guards by name.

Title: The evidence fetches declared a SPARQL prefix that matches nothing
Description: orchestrator/services/evidence/spatial_facts.py declared PREFIX ontosage: <http://ontosage.org/schema#>. The ontology's term namespace is <http://ontosage.org/capabilities#>. Measured live on bldg1: the declared IRI matches 0 triples, the real one 37,207. Five queries use the prefix - environmentalBoundary, zoneValidated, archivalIntervalS, calibratedOn, calibrationDueOn - so every one had returned nothing since it was written. Two scripts carried the same typo; propose_archival_intervals.py WRITES the intervals the completeness gate reads, so its output would have loaded cleanly and been invisible to the gate it exists to feed.
Root_Cause: A prefix pointing at an unused namespace produces valid SPARQL and an empty result. An OPTIONAL that never binds and a VALUES join that never matches raise nothing, so the failure is undetectable without checking the data by hand.
Fix_Approach: All three sites corrected to the real namespace. tests/test_ontosage_prefix_is_the_real_namespace.py scans orchestrator/, shared/ and scripts/ for the dead IRI and separately asserts that spatial_facts still queries all five terms, so removing one is a deliberate act rather than an accident.
Verification: Live after the fix: completeness returns 0.087 for a 7-day CO2 window (was "could not be established" every time) and calibration_state returns "expired" (was "unknown" every time). 3 unit tests.

Title: Spatial adequacy was never graded, so a wrong-room reading was never noticed
Description: Three independent breaks stopped the spatial gate ever producing a verdict, each silent. (1) facts_for_uuids reached the zone only via brick:isPointOf, while this building's sensors declare brick:hasLocation - the clause never bound for any sensor. (2) The zone-to-space hop matched only brick:feeds, while derive_zone_room_links.py asserts brick:hasPart - so the generated links were invisible. (3) The target space was resolved from entities[0] alone, and the dialogue emits the measurand first ('CO2 readings for Room 5.01' -> ['CO2','Room_5.01']), and with an underscore the graph does not use. Every room question therefore recorded spatial_adequacy 'none', which reads as 'no sensor covers the space asked about'.
Root_Cause: Four spellings of the same relationship across three modules and a generator, none of them wrong on its own. Every mismatch produced valid SPARQL and an empty OPTIONAL, so nothing raised and the resulting grade was indistinguishable from a genuine absence of coverage.
Fix_Approach: The zone hop accepts brick:isPointOf|brick:hasLocation and the zone-to-space hop accepts brick:feeds|brick:hasPart. resolve_space_iri normalises separators only (underscore, space, joined) - no building vocabulary, and an unmatched token still returns '' rather than guessing. Target resolution walks every entity and stops at the first that resolves unambiguously. Both remaining early returns now log WHY, because a silent return here is indistinguishable in the record from a real finding.
Verification: Live: 'What is the temperature in Room 3.17 right now?' now records 'spatial_adequacy: the reading is from Room4.66, which is not the space asked about' - the answer had been using a sensor in a different room and nothing said so. The CO2 question records 'a served zone links these spaces, but the link is not validated', the correct proxy grade. Advisory, so no answer changed.

Title: A register above the size limit was abandoned, and the fallback answered about something else
Description: _whole_register returned None whenever a register exceeded MAX_RECORD_ROWS (120). Falling back is correct; what followed was not. Measured live once the timetable was lifted into 675 sessions: "Which teaching sessions are scheduled in Room 1.06 this month?" was answered "the data you provided only lists spaces and the number of sensors in each area". Routing had already established the question was about TimetabledSession; that was discarded and the generated fallback asked about sensor counts, so a register holding the answer produced an answer about something else.
Root_Cause: The size check decided between "hand over the whole register" and "forget the register exists". There was no third option, and the question almost always carries its own scope.
Fix_Approach: An oversized register is now filtered by the identifiers the question names - a room number, a record code, a date - and handed over when the filtered set fits. NOTHING IS TRUNCATED: a question naming nothing specific ("which rooms have the most sessions?") still declines, because answering a superlative from an arbitrary 120 of 675 would look authoritative and be wrong. Aggregation for that shape is not built and is not claimed.
Verification: Live: the Room 1.06 question returns its 23 sessions from the 675-row register; "Which permits are open?" still returns the correct 3, so the small-register path is unregressed. 7 unit tests.

Title: "How many CO2 sensors are there?" answers 8 against a true 280
Description: Found incidentally while verifying BUG-427. The answer reasons: "The SPARQL results contain 72 rows, but each sensor is listed multiple times (once for each RDF type it is declared as)... there are 8 unique CO2 sensors." The graph holds 280 (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ?s) WHERE { ?s a brick:CO2_Sensor }). The model divided a LIMITed result set by its type multiplicity and produced a confident figure from a fraction of the data. NOT caused by this session's changes: the metrology guard does not match this question, verified.
Root_Cause: Same shape as CAVEAT-039, which this project already paid for once: a LIMIT with no DISTINCT, and a count computed by the model from whatever rows arrived rather than by the graph. A COUNT belongs in SPARQL.
Fix_Approach: Two-part. (1) _INVENTORY_RE now allows up to two class-qualifier words between "how many" and the noun, so a class-scoped count reaches a counting path instead of the generated-SPARQL path. (2) THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG IN A NEW WAY: it sent the question to the building-wide metrics snapshot, which reports the building totals and answered 2,721 - a different wrong number. The snapshot cannot filter by class; class_census can. The capability metrics path now defers when the question names a specific class, so the qualified form reaches the census and the bare form keeps the snapshot. A CONDITION qualifier (broken, offline, overdue) is excluded from both, because a census answering "how many sensors are broken?" with the total is BUG-427 in a different field.
Verification: Live on bldg1: "How many CO2 sensors are there?" now returns the class census including "CO2 Sensor - 280", the graph's true figure (was 8). "How many sensors are there?" still returns the building snapshot, and "How many sensors are overdue for calibration?" still returns 194 - neither regressed. 16 unit tests.

Title: A question spanning two registers is answered from one of them
Description: 'Which stakeholder groups are served by the accessibility team?' cannot be answered, while 'Which stakeholder groups does DEP-13 serve?' returns the correct three. The stakeholder register stores servedByDepartment as a CODE and the department directory holds the name; the whole-register handover passes ONE register to the model, so the join has nowhere to happen. The answer says so accurately - 'the department identifiers are not mapped to a department name' - which is honest and still a failure. || SECOND INSTANCE 2026-09-05, found by the regression probe: "I have back-to-back seminars in different rooms. Which transition needs the larger travel and setup time?" spans the circulation register (travel) and the workspace register (setup). The scorer picks ONE, and after "setup time" was added to WorkspaceProfile it picks that one and answers "we don't have explicit travel-time data" while the circulation register holds exactly that. Each register answers its half correctly in isolation. This is the same single-register limit as the department case, and it is now the shape of BOTH open failures in the probe.
Root_Cause: The register handover is deliberately single-class: it hands over one register with no generated SPARQL, which is what makes it reliable. A cross-register question needs either a join in the query or both registers in context, and neither exists.
Fix_Approach: NOT the obvious one. Denormalising the department name into the stakeholder register would fix this question and guarantee the two registers disagree within a year, which the mapping header already argues against. The options worth measuring are (a) resolving a named referent to its record id before scoping, so "the accessibility team" becomes DEP-13, or (b) handing over a second register when the scope tokens match one. Sized but not built.
Verification: Fixed by handing over a SECOND register when the question names two, not by denormalising fields between them. second_record_class() takes the runner-up only when it scores at least half the primary - "travel and setup" names both at 20 and 12, while a question merely mentioning "room" scores its second far below. The rows are merged with a `register` column and the guidance states plainly that the two registers are not interchangeable. Live: the transition question now returns Level 0 to Level 5, walking 9.5 min from the circulation register plus 5.0 min setup from the workspace register, total 14.5 - every figure verbatim from a row.

Title: A wide register returned an empty completion, and the user got nothing
Description: Found by the new live regression probe, not by any unit test. 'Which stakeholder groups are served by the accessibility team?' returned LLM-DEGRADED:empty_completion. The stakeholder register is 82 rows - comfortably inside MAX_RECORD_ROWS=120 - and 1,558 pivoted cells. MAX_RECORD_ROWS bounded the handover by rows while the prompt is paid for in rows TIMES columns, so the widest register in the building went into one prompt whole and the model returned nothing at all.
Root_Cause: A limit expressed in one unit against a requirement expressed in another - the same shape as several defects already in this tracker. A row limit cannot separate the failing register from the working ones: it has FEWER columns than two of them.
Fix_Approach: MAX_RECORD_CELLS, set from MEASUREMENT rather than estimate: stakeholder 1,558 fails, asset engineering 816, workspace 784, fire safety 600, department 460 all work, so 1000 sits between them. Measured AFTER the pivot, in the same unit as the budget. A cell-oversized register is RE-FETCHED scoped rather than declined. TWO OF MY OWN FIXES WERE WRONG FIRST: (1) a pre-check on an estimate from the mapping's columns understates real width by ~1.7x because every lifted record carries provenance predicates no mapping mentions - it declined the asset and workspace registers and took the probe from 23/25 to 19/25; (2) the cell check without a scoped retry was a dead end, so a merely-wide register was never scoped at all and 'which stakeholder groups does DEP-13 serve?' still failed.
Verification: Live: 'Which stakeholder groups does DEP-13 serve?' returns the correct three groups (was 'no such records appear in the triples supplied'). Regression probe 24/25, above the 23/25 baseline. 10 unit tests, including one asserting the budget sits between the largest working register and the failing one, and one asserting the measurement happens after the pivot.

Title: Every register answer was computed from the first TEN rows
Description: _format_results caps rows at `100 if show_all else 10`, where show_all requires the question to contain 'all', 'complete', 'full', 'everything' or 'list'. The deterministic whole-register handover exists PRECISELY so the model sees every record and can count, filter and group them - and it was seeing ten. Measured consequences: 'which departments have no out-of-hours route?' answered 7 on one run and 8 on another from a 20-row register (the truth is 8), and a merged two-register handover reported the second register 'isn't included in the snippet you posted' because its rows sat at positions 29 to 49. Found while investigating why a two-register merge appeared to have no effect; the cap had been silently shaping every register answer since the handover was built.
Root_Cause: A context-window protection applied in the wrong place and the wrong unit. The register path already bounds its size by MAX_RECORD_CELLS before the query runs; capping again at ten ROWS afterwards discarded the data the bound had just been calculated to permit.
Fix_Approach: _format_results takes an explicit row_limit, and both deterministic handovers pass one. The generic path keeps its old default, so nothing outside the register lane changes.
Verification: Live: 'which departments have no out-of-hours route?' now answers 'out of the 20 departments, 8 do not have' - the correct figure, stably. The two-register transition answer now quotes 9.5 minutes walking from the circulation register, which it previously said was not present.

Title: The deliberation decline knew why and how to fix it, and said neither
Description: A question over the 120-space fetch budget came back as 'I couldn't rank any spaces for this request. 1 spaces were excluded — see the evidence dossier.' The reason was recorded against the exclusion ('question spans 234 spaces, above the 120-space fetch budget') and the plan executor had ALREADY WRITTEN the remedy ('narrow it to a floor and I can answer it directly'). Neither reached the reader: EvidenceDossier had no field for the executor's notes and render_answer's empty branch printed a count. A reader could not tell a building with no such space from a question that was merely too broad, and only the second is fixable in one edit.
Root_Cause: Advice written, tested and unreachable — the same shape as the evidence gates and the observability lane before them. The dossier is a re-shaping of the outcome and simply had no field for this part of it.
Fix_Approach: EvidenceDossier carries guidance_notes from the outcome, and the empty-ranking branch states the distinct exclusion reasons and then the guidance. Rendered ONLY when nothing ranked, so successful answers are untouched.
Verification: Live: the over-budget question now answers 'Why: question spans 234 spaces, above the 120-space fetch budget' followed by 'Narrow it to a floor (Floor0..Floor5) or to a named room and I can answer it directly.' The narrowed form was then verified to work: 'Which space on Floor 3 has the best conditions for focused work this afternoon?' ranks Room 3.46, 3.17 and 3.14 with readings and names co2 as a gap — so the advice the decline gives is advice that pays off. Both shapes added to the regression probe.

Title: Pre-session readiness checks, on demand and on a schedule
Description: Requested by lecturers in the stakeholder capture: 'one concise, source-timestamped readiness check 30 minutes before each class'. Previously an honest decline - the system had no scheduled notification of any kind, and no path that joined the timetable, the AV register and the workspace register into one statement about a room.
Root_Cause: Not a defect. Every ingredient existed and nothing joined them at a useful moment.
Fix_Approach: services/readiness_check.py composes the check; a readiness_check intent, node and response-dispatch entry make it askable; a scheduler in the lifespan dispatches through the existing notification channels. THREE PROPERTIES ARE THE FEATURE: a source and a date on EVERY line (an undated line says 'date not recorded' rather than reading as current); the unknowns listed as prominently as the facts (a room with no AV record is not a room with working AV); and FOUR verdicts rather than two, because 'ready' and 'not ready' cannot express nothing-broken-and-nothing-checked. Building-agnostic, asserted by a test that greps the module for building vocabulary - which caught a live room number in my own docstring. The schedule is OFF by default and sends once per session, not once per sweep.
Verification: Live: 'Is Room 1.06 ready for my class?' returns the room's full label, five AV components dated 2026-08-28, the surveyed network and setup allowance dated 2026-09-01, and flags the untested hearing loop as the one blocker. 'Is Room 3.13 ready for my seminar?' returns 'no blockers found, with gaps' and states that no AV record names it. 18 unit tests, 2 regression-probe cases, docs/READINESS_CHECKS.md.

Title: A sixth heredoc backspace, and the guard that would have caught it scanned two directories
Description: _READINESS_RE was written through a bash heredoc; every  became a literal 0x08. The pattern compiled, read correctly in the file, printed identically in the terminal, and matched nothing - so the new lane was unreachable and two rounds of routing were debugged live before the bytes were inspected. tests/test_authority_contract.py already guards this, added after the fifth occurrence, and WOULD have caught it on the next full suite run - but it globbed orchestrator/services non-recursively, so agents/, workflow/ and scripts/ were never covered.
Root_Cause: Backslashes in a shell heredoc. The failure is invisible at every stage a human would look: the file, the diff and the terminal all render 0x08 as nothing.
Fix_Approach: Bytes repaired from a script file rather than a shell command, because the shell mangled the repair too. The guard now walks orchestrator/, shared/ and scripts/ recursively and requires more than 100 files scanned, so a glob that silently matches nothing fails. The durable lesson is in tasks/lessons.md: content with backslashes goes through the Edit tool or a script file, never a heredoc.
Verification: 0 backspace bytes across orchestrator/, shared/, scripts/ and tests/ (the one in test_authority_contract.py is the guard's own literal). Suite 5,004 pass.

Title: Fourteen asset statuses point at IRIs that have no triples, so every one answers 'not recorded'
Description: 'Is the lift working?' returns 'This building has no lifts recorded in its model.' bldg:status_lift_0 a ontosage:AssetStatus ; ontosage:statusOf bldg:Lift_Main IS in the graph, but bldg:Lift_Main has ZERO triples. A FILTER NOT EXISTS sweep shows this is not one asset: 14 of the building's 64 asset statuses (22%) name an untyped IRI - AccessibilitySummary, BikeStorage_Outdoor, Cafe_Ground, CybersecurityLab, Lift_Main (twice), Makerspace, NursingRoom_F2, PrayerRoom_104, Reception, ShowerFacility_F1, StudyArea_F1F2, Toilets_AllFloors, TradingRoom. Every one is an amenity an occupant or visitor would ask about, and every one has a status record written for it.
Root_Cause: The synthetic-status generator wrote a status for an asset it never declared, and asset_state_service._status_query opens with '?asset a ontosage:{class}' - so an untyped asset cannot match however many statuses point at it. Nothing validates that the object of a statusOf is a typed subject.
Fix_Approach: THREE PARTS, none sufficient alone. (1) DATA: input/bldg1_lifts.ttl declares the lift as the asset it is, transcribed from the same published accessibility survey the capability topic already cites -- and carries NO isSimulated flag, because the lift is real and only its status record is simulated. (2) STALE OUTPUT: the amenity-state file was the OLD generator's output, statusing an amenity set the building replaced; regenerated from the live graph, which drops the 13 stale names and statuses the 37 amenities that actually have a location. (3) GENERATOR: it now re-asserts each asset's own class alongside the status, so the file is correct ON ITS OWN rather than for as long as some other file keeps declaring the subject -- which is the dependency that broke -- and REFUSES to write a file that points a status at an undeclared subject. A fourth defect surfaced during the fix and is logged as BUG-451.
Verification: Live on the graph 2026-09-06: dangling statusOf 14 -> 0 of 58; assets carrying more than one status 1 -> 0; and asset_state_service._status_query's own SQL, run verbatim, returns Lift_Main / 'Main passenger lift' / operational / 2026-09-06T09:45:47 / lift_controller. 16 new offline tests in tests/test_a_status_names_an_asset_the_building_declares.py, which FAIL on the pre-fix tree (44 orphan subjects in one file, 1 in another) and which also found the SAME defect shape in bldg2, bldg3 and bldg4 -- so the class was never bldg1-specific. 316 existing asset/lift/status tests still pass. Live-confirmed 2026-09-07 through the chat API, cache flushed; see docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md.

Title: 174 CO2 sensors emit an air-quality-index band that the answer layer labels ppm
Description: 'Compare average CO2 on floor 1 versus floor 3 over the last week' answers 157 ppm vs 111 ppm and closes with a capital-expenditure recommendation. Outdoor air is about 420 ppm, so neither figure is a possible indoor reading. Traced: the floor 0-4 CO2 sensors resolve to sensor_data_floors04, where the last seven days read min 0.0, avg 74.1, max 150.0, and rows are still being written today. The narrow co2_data table is correct (400-1500, avg 788); the affected sensors are not in it. IT WAS NOT ONE MODALITY. Once the bands existed, a sweep of every narrow backend found 4,720,000 rows across EIGHT streams whose values were not measurements of the quantity they were filed under: the 174 CO2 sensors (0-150, an AQI scale); four colour-temperature points generating 18-28 when correlated colour temperature is measured in KELVIN, so a lighting question would have answered '22 K', three degrees above absolute zero; smoke and leak detectors -- binary devices -- generating 0-100; and four iaq_data CO2 sensors at 96.9% out of band. Each was a range chosen because it looked reasonable, with nothing tying it to what the instrument measures.
Root_Cause: input/bldg1_extended_narrow_uuids.json types 174 sensors as Air_Quality_Sensor with lo=0 hi=150 - an AQI band. The graph types the same UUIDs brick:CO2_Sensor and names them CO2_Level_Sensor_N.NN. The two sources disagree about the sensor's class and nothing compares them. NOTE: this is NOT the wide-table _WIDE_RANGES fallback that the external review blamed - that was corrected on 2026-09-03 and maps co2 to 400-1200. Fixing the file the review named would have changed nothing and been reported as done.
Fix_Approach: FOUR PARTS. (1) ONTOLOGY: ontology/measurand_kinds.ttl gains TWO bands per quantity -- ontosage:physicalMin/Max (what a reading CAN be, cited to NIOSH IDLH / WHO / definitional limits) and ontosage:typicalMin/Max (what a synthetic stream should generate). The distinction is load-bearing: 5,000 ppm of CO2 is an evacuation and it is still a reading, so a guard built on comfort limits would suppress exactly the readings a building most needs to report. 27 quantities, 52 sensor classes; supertypes (Air_Quality_Sensor, Gas_Sensor, Sensor, Point) are DELIBERATELY unmapped, because a band on a supertype reaches every instrument beneath it -- which is the defect itself. (2) GENERATOR: scripts/generate_publish_map.py, which did not exist, derives the map from the live graph and the declared bands. A sensor whose class declares no measurand is reported and SKIPPED, never given a default. (3) DATA: scripts/purge_implausible_readings.py removes rows that are not measurements -- see BUG-454 for the guard that stops it destroying the fault fixtures. (4) LANE: orchestrator/services/physical_bands.py + a gate in the SQL node, so every numeric lane downstream inherits it and an excluded reading is NAMED.
Verification: Live: the CO2 stream went 84 -> 86 -> 861 ppm across the publisher restart, in the same sensor's rows. 4,470,907 + 102,771 + 34,120 + 7,892 unit-error rows removed; 7,590 planted anomaly-fault sentinels (777.7 / 99999) verified intact afterwards. Publish map regenerated at 628 entries -- the same count as the hand-written one, with correct classes and bands. 16 offline tests across tests/test_a_generated_stream_carries_its_own_quantity.py and tests/test_an_impossible_reading_is_not_averaged.py, both of which reject the pre-fix map entry (Air_Quality_Sensor / 0..150) on two independent grounds. Full unit suite 5,039 pass, 44 skip, 0 fail. Live-confirmed 2026-09-07 through the chat API, cache flushed; see docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md.

Title: A structural spatial question is answered from cleaning and event registers, six rooms against forty-eight
Description: 'Which rooms are on floor 2?' routes to capability and returns six rooms, sourced from 'Cleaning Task Register, Public Event Register, Timetabled Sessions'. GraphDB holds 48 rooms on Floor2. The answer is not flagged as partial - it reads as the floor's room list.
Root_Cause: dialogue_agent runs a document-KB probe BEFORE classification and returns intent=capability whenever a document scores above the floor. It is guarded by 21 'and not' escape clauses, each added for a measured incident, and none covers a structural spatial question. A pre-LLM veto needing an exception per lane discovers each new shadowed lane only through a live wrong answer.
Fix_Approach: INVERTED, as planned. The document-KB prose probe no longer returns intent=capability before classification; it runs AFTER the classifier and the routing contract, in _promote_to_capability_from_documents, and only over an intent they left weak (general / general_knowledge / clarification / None). The nineteen 'and not' clauses are thereby made UNNECESSARY rather than merely deleted -- each was a regex reconstructing, badly, a judgement the classifier was about to make correctly. metadata and discovery are deliberately EXCLUDED from the overridable set even though the contract calls them weak: BUG-440 was precisely a structural question losing to a register, and a structural answer computed from the graph beats prose. The TTL-triples probe keeps its pre-LLM place -- it matches curated ontosage:layTerms exactly, so it is precise where prose is not, and no incident has implicated it. The 0.50 score floor is UNCHANGED, so a regression here can only be about sequencing and the two cannot be confused.
Verification: Live: 'Which rooms are on floor 2?' now routes to floor_plan and lists the floor's spaces with '+30 more' -- consistent with the 48 in GraphDB -- where it previously logged 'capability via document KB (3 chunk(s))' and returned six rooms from the Cleaning Task, Public Event and Timetabled Sessions registers. Full regression probe 50/50, including all 17 capability-bypass cases recorded under W1-1 for exactly this change, so the fix is not a silent trade. 34 offline tests, one per lane the clauses defended plus the LLM-outage path.

Title: Eight floors reported in a six-storey building, and more sensors reporting than exist
Description: 'How many sensors are there in total?' reports 'Floors: 8' alongside 'Mapped floor area 6,129 m2 across 6 floors' in the same answer, and 'Sensors declared 2,720' against 'Sensors that reported data in the last 24 h 2,763' - more instruments reporting than the model says exist.
Root_Cause: BOTH NUMBERS WERE CORRECT AND THE EXTERNAL REVIEW'S REMEDY WOULD HAVE MADE THE MODEL WORSE. It proposed retyping Rooftop and Parking_Level_Ground. But Brick 1.4 declares brick:Rooftop and brick:Parking_Level as subclasses of brick:Floor / brick:Storey, the building asserts exactly those specific types, and RDFS inference correctly derives 'a brick:Floor' for both -- verified by querying asserted types separately from inferred ones. Retyping would have made the model less accurate to satisfy a count. Likewise the sensor figures count different UNITS: 2,720 SUBJECTS typed brick:Sensor against 2,763 timeseries UUIDS, and a sensor may carry more than one reference (2,780 uuids sit on a brick:Sensor; 2,841 exist in the graph). Two adjacent lines using the same noun invited exactly the reading they got.
Fix_Approach: The COUNT says what it counted, which is the remedy this codebase already applies to Particulate_Matter_Sensor sweeping in TVOC (CAVEAT-286). Floors now render as '8 - 6 storeys plus 1 rooftop, 1 parking level (Brick counts these as floors)', with the breakdown read from the graph so a building with a mezzanine says mezzanine. The reporting line now says 'Data streams that reported' and states that it is not comparable to the sensor count. The breakdown query groups by ASSERTED type: a first version asked for the 'most specific' class via FILTER NOT EXISTS and returned two floors for a six-storey building, because Brick asserts Floor subClassOf Storey AND Storey subClassOf Floor -- 'most specific' is undefined inside a cycle.
Verification: Live against the graph: floor_kinds [('Floor',6),('Rooftop',1),('Parking_Level',1)], rendering 'Floors: 8 - 6 storeys plus 1 rooftop, 1 parking level'. 8 offline tests in tests/test_a_count_says_what_it_counted.py including one pinning the asserted-type grouping and one asserting a mezzanine building gets its own vocabulary. Full suite 5,062 pass. Live-confirmed 2026-09-07 through the chat API, cache flushed; see docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md.

Title: A governance question is refused as individual tracking because the pattern matches a bare 'and who'
Description: 'What is this building and who runs it?' routes to privacy_refusal: 'The system explains the building; it never tracks individuals.' The StakeholderGroup register that answers it holds 82 instances and never ran.
Root_Cause: INDIVIDUAL_PRESENCE_RE in services/privacy/inference_classes.py carries an alternative matching 'and'/'but' followed by 'who' with no presence predicate required. Any compound question whose second clause begins 'and who' is refused.
Fix_Approach: TWO CHANGES. (1) The bare clause is replaced by two shapes that are actually about identifying someone: a trailing '...and who?' (nothing follows, so the identity IS the question) and 'and who is/are/was/were' followed by a location word. (2) A governance allow-list -- who runs / manages / owns / operates / is responsible for / do I contact -- returns None BEFORE the presence rule, because an override placed after it could never fire. The allow-list requires the ABSENCE of any presence predicate rather than merely outranking it, so 'who manages this building and is she in her office right now?' stays refused: that is two questions and the second one is denied.
Verification: 12 shapes probed directly, 0 failures: eight governance questions now pass and four identification questions still refuse. 181 existing privacy/protect/leak tests pass unchanged; 16 new tests in tests/test_privacy_inference_classes.py, including one pinning the ORDER, since an allow-list after the presence rule is dead code. Live-confirmed 2026-09-07 through the chat API, cache flushed; see docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md.

Title: Developer-facing narration reaches the user in place of an answer
Description: 'Which rooms are stuffy right now?' returns 'I don't have the live CO2 or temperature readings that would let me tell you which rooms are currently stuffy' followed by a table of SENSOR COUNTS per space. The building has 589 air-quality sensors and a populated co2_data table. The model was handed a count query's results and narrated the shortfall.
Root_Cause: The generated SPARQL returned counts per space rather than readings, and nothing detects that an answer is describing its own inputs. No meta-answer guard exists.
Fix_Approach: grounding_guard.meta_answer_reason() plus a call at the END of the response node's dispatch, so any lane's prose is checked rather than one lane's. A match re-routes to _unanswered_response, which names the intent, the lanes that ran and what to try instead -- everything the narration was gesturing at, said in terms the reader can act on. THE HARD PART WAS NOT CATCHING IT: a bare 'I don't have X' cannot be the marker, because this system says exactly that in at least three legitimate deterministic declines ('I don't have a floor plan for Floor 7. Available floors: 0-5'), and suppressing those would destroy the honesty the project is built on. What made the stuffy-rooms answer a meta-answer was the PIVOT: having said it lacked the readings, it offered a substitute it had just labelled as not the thing asked for, then handed the task back. The markers are that pivot plus phrases naming the exchange itself ('the data you've provided', 'if you can run a query'). Honest declines are explicitly exempted by a second pattern set.
Verification: 16 prose samples probed directly, 0 failures: seven meta-answers caught (including the verbatim live failure) and nine honest declines and real answers untouched. 20 offline tests in tests/test_prose_about_the_pipeline_is_not_an_answer.py, two of which pin the WIRING and the guard's position after the whole dispatch. RESIDUAL: the underlying query defect is unfixed -- the generated SPARQL returned sensor COUNTS for a readings question -- so the stuffy question now declines honestly rather than answering. That needs a model to re-generate and verify; deferred. Live-confirmed 2026-09-07 through the chat API, cache flushed; see docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md.

Title: The floor-plan service invents room numbers when the PDF yields no text
Description: floor_plan_service falls back to generating rooms f'{floor}.{n:02d}' for n in 1..14 when PDF text extraction returns nothing. It fabricates referents, and it fabricates them in one building's numbering grammar.
Root_Cause: A convenience fallback written when an empty disambiguation prompt looked worse than a populated one. It violates contract 3 (no building literals) and contract 4 (never fabricate) simultaneously.
Fix_Approach: Return empty and say the plan could not be read. An empty list is a true statement; fourteen invented rooms are fourteen false ones.
Verification: 5 offline tests in tests/test_a_floor_plan_never_invents_a_room.py: an unreadable plan now returns [], a readable one returns only the rooms its text names, the caller's empty branch renders 'Which room or zone' rather than a zone list, and the constructing expression is pinned absent from the module's CODE (docstrings excluded via the AST -- the first version of that test failed on the fix's own explanation of the defect). Live-confirmed 2026-09-07 through the chat API, cache flushed; see docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md.

Title: The referent-existence gate has one call site in the whole orchestrator and fails open
Description: apply_referent_gate is invoked at exactly one place in orchestrator/workflow/_orchestrator.py. The register, asset_state, observability, readiness, diagnosis, deliberate, capability, spatial, floor_plan and analytics lanes all bypass it, and it fails open on exception. 'Temperature in Room 9.99?' also takes 46 seconds and blames the time rather than the absence.
Root_Cause: The gate was added to the lane where the fabrication was measured (BUG-189) and never generalised. An honesty guard that is lane-local protects one lane.
Fix_Approach: NOT A THIRD CALL SITE. The gate runs ONCE per turn, at the end of the dialogue node, before routing -- so every lane is covered by construction and a lane added next month needs no change. The helper's own docstring predicted the alternative: 'copying the block into each lane would have made the third copy the one that drifts'. Running once also costs one SPARQL round trip per turn instead of one per lane. A refusal short-circuits routing to `response` and is collected immediately after the privacy refusal, above every lane, because if the building does not contain the thing the question named then no lane can say anything true about it. Coverage is GATED_INTENTS (inherited, not copied) plus the standalone place lanes: register, asset_state, observability, readiness_check, diagnosis, deliberate, capability, spatial_query, floor_plan, events, alert, report, export. STILL FAILS OPEN, and logs when it does: refusing a legitimate question because GraphDB blinked is a worse trade than letting one through.
Verification: V12-02 LIVE RE-ASK 2026-09-10: CONFIRMED for what this row claims - the gate now RUNS on the sensor_data lane, which was the point. Q 'What is the CO2 level in room 9.99 right now?' -> 'I couldn't verify 9.99 against Abacws Building's model just now - the existence check didn't complete in time. Rather than risk attributing another sensor's readings to it, I'd rather you ask again in a moment.' It fired and FAILED SAFE rather than fabricating. DEGRADED OUTCOME, tracked separately: the existence check timed out (121.4s), so the user is told to retry instead of being told the room does not exist. That is BUG-499.  ||  PRIOR: 8 offline tests in tests/test_the_referent_gate_covers_every_lane.py pinning the call, the routing short-circuit, the dispatch ORDER against three lanes that would otherwise pre-empt it, the lane coverage, the inheritance of GATED_INTENTS rather than a second

Title: building_context reads two keys that no building.yaml in this repo writes
Description: shared/building_context.py resolves the prefix from 'building_prefix' and the timezone from 'building_timezone'. bldg2/3/4 write 'ontology_prefix'; bldg1 writes NEITHER key and no timezone at all. Every building therefore silently runs on the env default, and a building whose prefix genuinely differs would be misread with no error.
Root_Cause: The reader and the writers were written against different key names and nothing asserts they agree.
Fix_Approach: The resolver reads `ontology_prefix`/`timezone` first -- the keys the buildings actually write -- and still honours the older spellings so an existing file keeps working. Separately, the buildings now STATE their identity: bldg1 gained `ontology_prefix` and `timezone` (it had neither), bldg2 and bldg3 gained `timezone`. A default that is right for one building is a trap for the next.
Verification: bldg2/3/4 now resolve their declared prefix instead of the env default. 11 offline tests in tests/test_a_building_states_its_own_identity.py, including one asserting the declared prefix is the one the building's own TTL binds -- a declaration that is present and wrong is worse than an absent one, because it silences the fallback while still being wrong.

Title: The project's own vocabulary is missing from its own SPARQL pre-flight
Description: sparql_validator._PREFIX_INJECT declares rdf, rdfs, owl, brick, ref and ashrae. Neither ontosage: nor hbco: is present, so a generated query using either fails validation unless the model happens to emit the PREFIX itself.
Root_Cause: The inject list predates both vocabularies and was never extended when they landed.
Fix_Approach: ontosage: and hbco: added, plus s223: (the same namespace as ashrae:, spelled both ways across this project's TTL and prompts), skos:, unit: and rec:.
Verification: Full suite 5,114 pass; no query shape regressed.

Title: Six per-building config loaders search only the nested layout, which the flat layout never produces
Description: rules.yaml, channels.yaml, recipes.yaml and goals.yaml were each loaded by a hand-written search that looked ONLY at input/<building_id>/<file>. The canonical layout is FLAT -- under swap-by-rename the active building's files sit directly in input/, and the nested form exists nowhere in this repo. RAISED TO P1 ON MEASUREMENT: input/rules.yaml and input/channels.yaml BOTH EXIST for the active building and neither was ever loaded, so the ECA rules engine and notification dispatch have been dark for every building. The log line was 'no rules.yaml for building bldg1 -- feed framework idle', which reads exactly like a building that chose not to configure any.
Root_Cause: shared/building_paths.resolve_building_file has existed for this since the flat layout landed and tries nested then flat. Ten files used it; the same logic was written five more times, and every copy was wrong. 'Absent' and 'present but unreachable' produced the same log line, so nothing distinguished them.
Fix_Approach: Four loaders now delegate to the one resolver, keeping their literal templates only as a fallback for a caller with neither layout under a standard root.
Verification: input/rules.yaml and input/channels.yaml now resolve through both engines' own _find_yaml. 7 offline tests in tests/test_per_building_config_is_found_in_either_layout.py, including one that SKIPS when a file is absent and FAILS when it is present-but-unreachable -- the distinction the log could not make. Full suite 5,121 pass.

Title: The new-building command passes a flag the script rejects and queries a repository that does not exist
Description: .claude/commands/new-building.md calls 'onboard_building.py --building-id <id>'; the script's parser accepts --id. The same command and deploy-check.md both query http://localhost:7200/repositories/ontosage/sparql; the live repository is 'bldg'. Separately, .env.example is missing exactly 31 settings the live .env uses, and './data/bldg1:/staging:ro' is mounted by docker-compose.yml AND the bldg2, bldg3 and bldgtest compose files - so one building's staging directory follows every other building.
Root_Cause: Command files and compose files were copied per building and never re-derived from the scripts they call.
Fix_Approach: FOUR THINGS. (1) `/new-building` calls `--id` (the flag the parser accepts) with `--name` and `--namespace`, which non-interactive mode requires -- a building without them inherits the previous building's identity. (2) Both command files query repository `bldg`; `ontosage` exists on no deployment, so the step could only return an error and its gate read that as a failed build. (3) `.env.example` gained all 31 missing settings, secrets as PLACEHOLDERS never values. (4) The `./data/bldg1:/staging:ro` mount is removed from all four compose files -- it named ONE building in every one of them, including bldg2's and bldg3's, and was dead anyway: data/bldg1/ is empty and nothing in rag-service reads /staging.
Verification: `docker compose config -q` still validates. Key parity is asserted by tests/test_env_example_documents_what_the_system_uses.py, which SKIPS when no live .env exists and fails on any live setting the template omits.

Title: What the external V10 review got wrong, recorded so it is not re-adopted
Description: The review is substantially correct - 29 structural claims and all five live failures reproduced. Three claims did not survive verification and are recorded here because they are plausible enough to be re-adopted from the document later: (1) it blames the CO2 defect on mysql_dummy_publisher._WIDE_RANGES, which was already fixed and maps co2 to 400-1200 - the proposed fix is a no-op, see BUG-439 for the real path; (2) '34 of 39 record classes have zero TTL instances in every building' is false for bldg1, where 36 of 40 discovered classes carry instances and only the three event classes are empty; (3) '~800 hard-coded strings' is unsupported - its own audit found 141 raw hits and 15 real defects, and the 800 appears to count every string inside every regex and frozenset, which conflates literals with vocabulary coupling and makes the real finding harder to act on. Smaller: the few-shot library is at orchestrator/data/ not data/; Path('input') sites number 33 not 60+; the referent gate has one call site not two; the capability short-circuit has 21 escape clauses not 16 (worse than claimed); and the accessible-toilet question failed differently than described.
Root_Cause: A review is measurement, and in this project the measurement apparatus has been wrong more often than the system. The reviewer's errors are the same shape as the ones this project keeps making: a cause inferred from the code that looks responsible rather than from the data that is wrong.
Fix_Approach: No fix. Recorded as context for anyone reading V10_REVIEW_AND_PLAN.md directly.

Title: Two status records for one asset produced a coin toss with a fresh-looking date
Description: asset_state_service._status_query is documented as 'latest status per asset' and does not compute one: MAX(?t) takes the newest observation date while SAMPLE(?v) takes an arbitrary value, so an asset with two records answers with the NEWEST DATE beside a possibly OLDER VALUE. That is worse than reporting a stale status honestly, because the fresh date makes the stale value read as current. Exposed while fixing BUG-438: declaring the building's lift made it both an ontosage:Lift and a located ontosage:Amenity, so two generator families each wrote it a status -- 'operational' from the lift controller and 'out_of_service' from the estates helpdesk. 'Is the lift working?' became a coin toss, and neither answer would have mentioned that a second source disagreed.
Root_Cause: GROUP BY with independent aggregates. The GROUP BY was added for a real reason (a two-label fan-out once reported fourteen floors in a six-storey building) and the aggregates were chosen per column without asking whether they would still describe one record.
Fix_Approach: TWO LAYERS. Data: the generator now writes one status record per asset -- the status family owns lifts because a lift controller outranks a helpdesk, and the amenity family yields, by CLASS so it holds for any building. Lane: the query counts the distinct values it collapsed and concatenates them, and an asset whose records disagree is reported as UNCONFIRMED rather than as working, with the conflicting values named. An accessibility asset presented as working on a coin toss strands somebody.
Verification: The new query shape runs against GraphDB and returns value_count=1 / all_values='operational' for the building's one lift. Three offline tests in tests/test_asset_state_lane.py cover the disputed case, the ordinary case, and the query itself still asking for the count; 54 pass in that file. A fourth test in tests/test_a_status_names_an_asset_the_building_declares.py pins one-status-per-asset across every building's TTL.

Title: The sensor-to-timeseries link is written three ways and the code follows one
Description: Joining sensors to their timeseries references returned 522 rows where the building has 628, and the missing 106 looked like orphan references with no sensor at all. They are not orphans. The link is expressed in three vocabularies: s223:hasExternalReference reaches 2,763 sensors and 2,839 uuids, ref:hasExternalReference reaches 2,727 and 2,733, and brick:hasExternalReference reaches 2. The code spells 'ref:' at 43 sites and 'ashrae:' at 9, so 106 uuids -- an entire synthetic modality set, with rows landing in MySQL right now -- are invisible to most of the system. This also explains part of the 'declared 2,720 vs reporting 2,763' inconsistency in BUG-441.
Root_Cause: Design contract 8 broken in the subtlest available way: both halves are present -- the sensor is in the graph AND its rows are in a registered database -- and the join between them is written in a vocabulary the reader does not speak. Nothing errors; the sensors simply do not exist as far as most lanes are concerned. The affected references are BLANK NODES, so no TTL file could have repaired them from outside.
Fix_Approach: scripts/normalise_timeseries_links.py asserts the canonical predicate wherever only an alias exists, into its own named graph so the building's source files stay as their author wrote them and one DROP undoes it. Idempotent, and no namespace or identifier appears in it. Asserting rather than rewriting 43 query sites is deliberate: both vocabularies are legitimate and 2,727 references already carry both, so this makes the exception match the rule. Rewriting the readers would leave the 44th, written next month, wrong again.
Verification: 127 links normalised, 127 -> 0 unreachable. The publish-map generator then saw 628 sensors instead of 522, matching the hand-written map exactly.

Title: Six occupancy points claimed to measure two different quantities
Description: bldg:Occupancy_Sensor_Floor0..5 were typed as BOTH brick:Occupancy_Count_Sensor and brick:Occupancy_Sensor. In Brick 1.4 these are siblings under brick:Sensor, not a class and its subclass: one detects presence (binary), the other counts people. A question about either could be answered with a reading of the other. The label ('Occupancy Count Sensor - Floor N') and the unit (unit:NUM) both say count, so the presence type was the surplus assertion.
Root_Cause: Belt-and-braces typing at authoring time. The input validator has checked for exactly this since CAVEAT-286 and could not see it: the check needs a measurand declaration per class, and neither occupancy class had one until V10 W1-3 declared 27 quantities. The validator was right and had nothing to reason with.
Fix_Approach: brick:Occupancy_Sensor removed from the six subjects that also assert the count type. The validator now fails on any recurrence, in any building, because both classes now declare a measurand.
Verification: tests/test_measurand_typing.py 15 pass (6 failing before). TTL reparses at 371 triples and is reloaded into the graph.

Title: The plausibility purge would have deleted the anomaly graders' planted faults
Description: scripts/purge_implausible_readings.py, as first written, deleted every row outside its quantity's declared physical band. scripts/grade_anomalies.py 'inject' plants labelled faults by writing sentinel values -- 777.7 for a stuck sensor, 99999 for a spike, value+500 for a drift -- PRECISELY BECAUSE they are implausible. Run as written, the purge would have deleted the faults, left the labels, and reported every detector as having missed everything. 7,590 rows were at risk across five tables.
Root_Cause: The FIFTH time in this project's history that a measurement apparatus was about to be broken by a fix to the thing it measures. The band tells you a value is not a measurement; it does not tell you whether that is a scale error or an event, and only the first is safe to delete.
