Fix_Approach: The rule is a SHARE, per stream. A stream where nearly every row is out of band is a unit error -- the instrument never measured that quantity on that scale. A stream where a minority is out of band contains events, and those rows are the signal. Default threshold 95%, adjustable, and below it the rows are reported and left alone. The threshold started on the band GROUP and that hid the truth too: iaq_data's six CO2 sensors averaged 72.8% and nothing was touched, while per stream four were 96.9% (a clean scale error) and two were 39.5% (wrong until a date). A unit error belongs to an instrument, not to a quantity. Streams that are PARTLY out of band are named in the output rather than silently skipped.
Verification: After purging 4.72M unit-error rows, a sweep of every table with a value column confirms 7,590 sentinel rows (777.7 / 99999) intact across co2_data, humidity_data, light_data, noise_data and plant_data.

Title: A pronoun asking where a person is passed every privacy rule
Description: 'Is he at his desk?' and 'Is she in the building?' were classified as no inference at all and reached the data lanes. The person vocabulary listed roles (professor, manager, colleague, the person) and no PRONOUNS, and every presence alternative requires a person word -- so the most natural way to ask where a named individual is, once the name has been said, matched nothing. Found while narrowing the over-broad 'and who' clause (BUG-442); confirmed against the pre-change file, so it is not a regression from that work.
Root_Cause: A vocabulary built from the leak-benchmark traps, which spell the role out. Real conversation introduces a person once and uses a pronoun thereafter, so the gap sits exactly where a multi-turn conversation puts it.
Fix_Approach: he/she/him/her added to the person vocabulary. 'they' and 'it' are excluded on purpose: 'are they in the meeting room?' is how people ask about a delivery, a meeting or a set of sensors, and refusing those protects nobody. Safe because every alternative using the person vocabulary also requires a presence predicate nearby, so a pronoun alone never triggers a refusal.
Verification: 'Is he at his desk?' and 'Is she in the building?' now classify as individual_presence; 'Are they in the meeting room?' and 'Is it in the lab?' still classify as None. Covered by parametrised tests in tests/test_privacy_inference_classes.py.

Title: The dangling-reference validator could not see full-IRI declarations
Description: Extending validate_dangling_references to ontosage: relations (V10 W1-2) immediately reported 19 amenities across bldg1, bldg2 and bldg3 as declared nowhere. Every one was declared -- as a FULL IRI on its own line, '<http://.../abacws#Amenity_StudyArea_Floor0>\n    a ontosage:Amenity ;' -- and _DECLARATION_RE recognised prefixed names only. With the check limited to brick: predicates the gap had never shown, because the files using brick: relations happen to write their subjects prefixed.
Root_Cause: Turtle admits two notations for a subject and the matcher knew one. The blind spot was invisible for as long as the check's scope happened to avoid it.
Fix_Approach: The matcher reads both notations and compares on LOCAL NAMES, so a subject written 'bldg:X' in one file and '<http://.../X>' in another is one node. Shipped together with the extension that exposed it: a validator that cries wolf is one people switch off, and it would have taken the real findings with it.
Verification: All four buildings clean. 10 offline tests in tests/test_a_relation_points_at_something_declared.py, which PLANT the defect in a fixture rather than asserting the tree is clean -- a check that passes everywhere may simply be broken, and the original was.

Title: A building is a directory with a building.yaml, not one holding TTL
Description: New checks discovered buildings by globbing 'bldg*' for any directory containing TTL. That swept in bldg2_source/ and bldg3_source/ -- the original vendor exports, tens of thousands of triples the system never loads -- and reported a dangling 'bldg:chiller' in bldg2_source/bldg2.ttl as a build failure.
Root_Cause: The convention that names a building folder ('bldg<N>') also names its staging folder ('bldg<N>_source'). Presence of building.yaml is what actually distinguishes them, and the rest of the system already uses it.
Fix_Approach: Every new check requires building.yaml. A check that reports defects in data nobody loads is a check people learn to skip, and it would have taken the real findings with it.
Verification: Three test files rescoped; the chiller false positive is gone and all buildings pass.

Title: The strict-secrets boot guard covered five of about fourteen credentials
Description: Filling .env.example (CAVEAT-449) made a second problem visible: SIX credentials held values IDENTICAL to the committed example -- POSTGRES_PASSWORD, PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD, API_KEY, API_PGPASSWORD, API_MYSQL_PASSWORD, PG_THINGSBOARD_PASSWORD -- and STRICT_SECRETS, whose entire purpose is to refuse startup on an unchanged credential, had nothing to say about any of them. Its list was five names, kept by hand.
Root_Cause: TWO gaps, and only one is fixable by editing the list. First, drift: a hand-kept list does not grow when a credential does. Second, and structural: those six are read by docker-compose directly and never become Settings fields, so no amount of work on the field list reaches them.
Fix_Approach: The list is DERIVED from the Settings fields whose names look like credentials, so one added next month is covered without anyone remembering. For the compose-only six, the guard compares the process environment against .env.example -- which IS the template, and which this module already treats as exactly as insecure as a shipped default when left unfilled. Best-effort: a missing .env.example is not a reason to refuse to boot. All three placeholder spellings (CHANGE-ME, CHANGE_ME, YOUR_) are now recognised; matching one left the other two looking like real values.
Verification: Probed directly: setting POSTGRES_PASSWORD to its .env.example value with STRICT_SECRETS=true now refuses startup and names the key. 7 offline tests in tests/test_the_secrets_guard_covers_what_it_claims.py. NOT CHANGED: the six live values on this development machine, which runs STRICT_SECRETS=false -- rotating a Postgres password without recreating its volume breaks auth, and that is the user's call, not a fix to apply silently.

Title: Plant diagnosis queried one building's table for points stored in seven
Description: anomaly/diagnosis.py built its plant candidates with a literal `stored_at: "plant_data"`. The external review called this 'plant diagnosis dark elsewhere', and measurement makes it worse: this building's plant points are spread across SEVEN storage keys -- database1 (478), plant_data (44), database1_synth (8), occupancy_data, light_data, water_data, equipment_data. So the literal was wrong on bldg1 too, for every plant point outside one table, and the lane returned empty with no error.
Root_Cause: The storage key was invented at the point of use rather than read. The graph already carries `ref:storedAt` on every timeseries reference; the plant query simply did not ask for it.
Fix_Approach: PlantPoint gains `stored_at`, projected from the point's own `ref:storedAt`. Empty when the point declares none, and the caller then routes by its default rather than guessing a table name.
Verification: 121 plant/diagnosis unit tests pass; the literal is gone from the tree and check_building_literals.py has a `datasource key literal` rule that fails on its return.

Title: Three prompts and a repair path taught a namespace that resolves to nothing
Description: `self_correction_engine.apply()` -- the LAST thing a user's question touches when every correction strategy has failed -- defaulted the namespace to `http://example.com/building#`. The rag-service's few-shot SPARQL examples declared `PREFIX ex: <http://example.org/building#>` in three places. A placeholder namespace matches nothing in any graph, so a query built on it returns ZERO ROWS AND NO ERROR -- indistinguishable from a building that has no such sensors, and arriving precisely where a user is least able to tell.
Root_Cause: A placeholder that LOOKS like configuration. Unlike a missing value it never raises, and unlike a wrong value it never returns anything to contradict.
Fix_Approach: The repair path resolves the active namespace and DECLINES when it cannot, rather than emitting a query with no namespace filter (which would sweep every building in a shared repository). The rag-service prompts substitute the building's own prefix and namespace through a non-brace marker -- `{building_ns}` inside a ChatPromptTemplate would become a required input variable and break every caller.
Verification: Probed with BUILDING_NAMESPACE set to a synthetic value: both rag-service prompts render with it and no example.org string survives. Suite 5,130 pass.

Title: An accessibility question was declined while the building held the answer
Description: 'Nearest accessible toilet to room 3.10?' answered 'No toilet is reachable from 3.10 in the floor-plan adjacency data.' The floor-plan adjacency really could not answer it. The BUILDING could: a toilet on that very floor, and two VERIFIED accessible WCs on Floor 4 and Floor 0 -- none on Floor 3. For someone with mobility needs 'no toilet is reachable' and 'the accessible one is one floor up' are not degrees of the same answer; the first ends a journey.
Root_Cause: The nearest-amenity path had exactly one source. When floor-plan geometry came back empty it declined, and never asked the amenity catalogue -- which is where a building that has no drawn adjacency still records what it has and where.
Fix_Approach: services/amenity_proximity.py, consulted AFTER the adjacency search and never instead of it: a surveyed route beats a floor count whenever one exists. It orders amenities of the asked kind by how many floors away they are, states plainly when the asker's OWN floor has none, and says in every answer that floors apart is not walking distance and does not account for door types or whether the lift is in service. An amenity whose floor the building does not record sorts LAST, not nearest: treating unknown as here is how a confident wrong answer is built.
Verification: Live against the graph: the accessible question now answers 'There is no accessible toilet recorded on Room 3.10's floor. The nearest is Accessible WC - Floor 4 - 1 floor up', and the non-accessible question still finds the toilet on Floor 3. 22 offline tests. Closes V7-T23. Live-confirmed 2026-09-07 through the chat API, cache flushed; see docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md.

Title: The first fix for BUG-461 called every toilet accessible, from its lay terms
Description: The amenity fallback decided accessibility by searching for 'accessible', 'wheelchair' and similar across each amenity's lay terms. Every ordinary toilet in this building carries 'toilet, toilets, washroom, restroom, bathroom, wc, accessible toilet' -- lay terms exist so somebody TYPING those words finds a toilet. So the fallback reported 11 of 12 amenities as accessible and told a wheelchair user the toilet on their own floor was usable, when the accessibility register records verified accessible WCs only on floors 0 and 4. Caught by probing the live graph before wiring it in.
Root_Cause: A search vocabulary read as an assertion. Lay terms answer 'what might somebody call this?'; they never answer 'what is it?'. The distinction is invisible until a lay term happens to name a PROPERTY rather than the thing.
Fix_Approach: Accessibility is read from the DECLARED fact -- ontosage:accessibilityVerified true on an ontosage:AccessibilityFeature -- and from nothing else. UNVERIFIED IS NOT ACCESSIBLE, which is the accessibility register's own stated doctrine and the reason the property exists. Pinned by two tests that fail if a lay term is ever consulted again.
Verification: Re-probed live: the accessible query returns exactly the two verified WCs, and the ordinary query still returns all twelve toilets.

Title: The routing rules do not yet consult the building lexicon
Description: services/building_lexicon.py is built, tested (25 offline tests over three room grammars) and populated at boot -- the live building logs '429 measurand word(s), 31 space noun(s), 5 identifier shape(s)'. The routing layer does NOT read it yet: _ROOM_ID_RE, _ZONE_ID_RE, _SENSOR_ID_RE, _DATA_ANALYTIC_WORDS, _SPACE_NOUNS and _MODALITY_STOPWORDS still carry their hand-written values.
Root_Cause: NOT AN OVERSIGHT -- a sequencing decision. Swapping a routing regex changes which lane a question takes, and the 33-case regression probe exists to catch exactly the silent trade that follows: a guard added for one shape quietly taking another with it. The probe needs a live model, and the local GPU was committed elsewhere. Landing the swap unverified would repeat BUG-431's first fix, which corrected one question and started answering another with the building-wide total.
Fix_Approach: Consume the lexicon ADDITIVELY -- generic list OR lexicon, never lexicon alone, because 'temperature' and 'last week' are domain English and a building whose graph is still loading must not lose them. Extend the probe with a case per affected rule FIRST, then swap, then re-run. Ships with the same discipline W1-1/W0-2 are waiting on.
Verification: Owed: 33-case regression probe plus new per-rule cases, on a live model. Until then routing behaviour is unchanged, which is the point.

Title: The plausibility band map was silently truncated to 1,000 sensors
Description: The log read '1000 sensor(s) carry a declared physical band'. That is not a count -- it is SPARQLAgent._execute_query's LIMIT 1000 safety cap, correct for a model-generated query and wrong for an exhaustive map. The gate therefore had nothing to say about 65% of the building's 2,841 instrumented uuids. The symptom was a RIGHT-LOOKING answer: the floor comparison reported 797 ppm against 775 ppm -- both plausible, both a vast improvement on the 157/111 that started this -- while a sensor reading 190 ppm was folded into the average, because its uuid fell outside the truncated map. The model happened to flag it as anomalous, which is luck, not the guard.
Root_Cause: A safety cap applied to a query that is not a search. A cap on an exhaustive query does not fail; it under-reports -- and under-reporting from a GUARD reads exactly like having nothing to report.
Fix_Approach: The band query carries its own LIMIT 100000, and the loader announces a count that is an exact multiple of 1,000 as suspicious, because the round number in the log was the only thing that revealed this.
Verification: Live: band coverage 1,000 -> 2,281; '1000 reading(s) excluded as physically impossible across 1 sensor(s)'; the comparison moved to 835 vs 790 ppm. Two offline tests pin the explicit LIMIT and the suspicious-count warning.

Title: A curly apostrophe defeated the meta-answer guard
Description: The guard shipped with 20 passing offline tests and the FIRST live re-ask returned the exact prose it exists to suppress. Two gaps: 'What I can give you is' was absent from a pivot list holding share/tell you/offer; and “If you’d like to check ... just let me know” never matched, because the model wrote a RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK where the pattern expects an apostrophe.
Root_Cause: A class, not an instance. A model writes curly quotes, en dashes and em dashes wherever prose calls for them, so EVERY pattern matching a contraction or a dash in model output had the same hole. Offline fixtures are typed in ASCII, so no offline test could have found it.
Fix_Approach: Typography is normalised once before matching -- a translation table rather than another alternative added to one regex -- and the pivot verb list widened to any verb that hands over a substitute. The live answer is now a fixture.
Verification: Live: 'which rooms are stuffy right now?' now returns the honest decline naming the intent and the lane that ran. 29 offline tests, including the verbatim live answer and a curly/straight equivalence check.

Title: A room identifier was read as a floor number: 3.10 became floor ten
Description: 'Nearest accessible toilet to room 3.10?' answered 'The nearest is Accessible WC - Floor 4 - 6 floors down.' Floor 4 is ONE FLOOR UP from floor 3. Space carries no floor field -- the floor lives on the MANIFEST -- so the fallback, the trailing number of the zone id, was the only branch that ever ran, and 3.10's trailing number is 10. Introduced by the W0-7 fix the day before.
Root_Cause: A grammar guess where an authoritative source exists. Every offline test passed because each supplies from_floor directly; none exercised the derivation -- the classic shape of a defect only an end-to-end ask finds.
Fix_Approach: The floor is read from the manifest that contains the space. A caller that cannot supply one passes None, and the answer then says the floor is not recorded rather than computing a distance from a number it guessed.
Verification: Live: 'The nearest is Accessible WC - Floor 4 (Fourth Floor) - 1 floor up.' Two offline tests pin the manifest as the source and the None-means-unknown behaviour.

Title: The floor-comparison question is slow, and once returned degenerate text
Description: 'Compare average CO2 on floor 1 versus floor 3 over the last week' fetches about 1.8M rows across ten tables. Observed at 63s, 94s, and twice past the probe's 121s client timeout. On a run with a 7-minute timeout the model returned a wall of '3.04? not present. 3.05? not present.' -- reasoning leakage on a long prompt, the BUG-188 class. NOT introduced by the V10 work: the same question answered correctly at 63s and 94s on the same build.
Root_Cause: A breadth question whose fetch is not bounded before it reaches the prompt. V7-T24 already tracks this shape.
Fix_Approach: The LATENCY is not fixed; the TOTAL LOSS is. Analytics repairs now run inside a time budget derived from WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_S (half of it), so the lane stops retrying while there is still time to narrate instead of consuming the whole request and dying with nothing. Derived rather than written down separately: two deadlines in two files that cannot see each other is BUG-473 exactly. Every LLM call in the lane is now timed and sized in the log -- the 420s run had SIX MINUTES with no log line between the code executor returning and the deadline, so the lane could not be told apart from a hang. The real latency fix is a deterministic path for common aggregates: config/recipes.yaml already holds 41 recipes including co2_average, and they are injected into the code prompt as TEXT rather than executed, so the LLM still writes the loop. That is a change to the lane answering most data questions and was not landed hours before a demo.
Verification: Three consecutive live runs after the change: 61.3s, 67.3s, 58.7s, all OK, against 63/87/109s and one 420s timeout before. HONEST CAVEAT: none of those three needed a repair, so they do not demonstrate the budget firing -- they show the question is usually fine, which was already known. What the budget guarantees is that the slow case ends in an answer rather than silence. 8 offline tests cover the budget itself, including that a FAST failure still uses every attempt (the bound must not cost an answer repairs would have found).

Title: The heuristic grader never read the question, and credited a number as any answer
Description: corpus_replay._heuristic_grade said so in its own docstring: 'the question is currently unused by the heuristic but kept for parity with the LLM judge'. Every test in it examines the shape of the RESPONSE, so an answer containing digits was credited answered-with-data whatever the digits were about. 'When was the fume cupboard last tested?' answered with a table of sensor counts scored the same as a date. The withdrawn rows include 'That question reaches 288 sensors -- more than I can read in one request' and 'I can't complete that request as asked'.
Root_Cause: A grader written from the answers it had seen rather than from the contract it was scoring. NOT a re-capture problem, which is how it was first scoped: the 2,960-row baseline holds questions and answers and NO grade column, so grading is a separate pass and the fix re-grades rows already on disk.
Fix_Approach: A narrow, generous question-shape check applied only where a CREDIT is about to be given: does the answer contain the KIND of thing the question asked for -- any date-ish token, any role-ish word -- never whether it is the right one. Judging correctness is the LLM judge's job and a regex that tried would be worse than the gap it closes. A demotion goes to `deflected`, not `wrong`: the response is not false, it does not answer.
Verification: Re-graded the capture on disk, answers unchanged: answered-with-data 1311 -> 1297 (-14, 0.5% of the corpus), deflected 257 -> 271. 26 offline tests. THE FIRST VERSION WITHDREW 28 ROWS AND HALF OF THEM WRONGLY -- see CAVEAT-469.

Title: The first grader fix withdrew credit from answers that were correct
Description: Matching a bare `when` and a bare `who` flagged 53 rows and moved 28. Most `when` in this corpus is a SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTION and most `who` a RELATIVE pronoun: 'which assets are overdue WHEN approved regimes diverge', 'is heat recovery effective WHEN conditions permit', 'a staff member WHO is officially available', 'conditions constrain WHO may work on this'. None asks for a date or a role.
Root_Cause: A question WORD is not a question. Leading position is not the discriminator either: 'When a lift is unavailable, how much capacity is left?' begins with the word and asks about capacity.
Fix_Approach: `when` must be followed by an auxiliary or modal (was/is/did/should/can/...); `who` must open a clause -- sentence start, or after a comma or `and`. 53 matches fell to 34, and the withdrawal from 28 rows to 14.
Verification: Seven conjunction/relative fixtures verbatim from the capture assert no withdrawal; eight interrogative fixtures assert the check still fires. A grader that under-credits is exactly as wrong as one that over-credits, and harder to notice because the number moves the flattering way.

Title: A draft answer outranked every lane that had actually computed one
Description: `dialogue_response` was checked SECOND in the response dispatch, above the register, asset-state, events, diagnosis, deliberation, analytics and SQL lanes. Any node that wrote a draft -- the dialogue node's generic reply, a greeting, a locked-capability notice -- pre-empted a richer result computed in the same turn.
Root_Cause: It had to be high once: three lanes (self_description, general_knowledge, locked_capability) write their REAL answer into that key and have no other. Those are standalone intents that route straight to `response`, so no computed lane runs beside them -- the constraint was real and the position was a stronger conclusion than it supported.
Fix_Approach: Moved to last, above the honest-decline fallback. The three lanes still deliver their answers; the draft simply no longer outranks work that happened. A CLARIFICATION was briefly promoted to the top instead and that was wrong -- see CAVEAT-471.
Verification: 33-case regression probe 33/33; unit suite 5,257 pass.

Title: Promoting clarifications above the computed lanes hid a correct answer
Description: The first version of the W2-6 reorder kept clarifications at the TOP, reasoning that asking a question back is a decision not to answer, so overriding it with a guess would be a substitution. The probe disagreed: 'Which space on Floor 3 has the best conditions for focused work this afternoon?' came back as 'Which floor did you mean? I know: Floor0 ... Floor3', hiding a ranking the deliberate lane had produced.
Root_Cause: The reasoning ignored a structural fact: the disambiguation path in `_dialogue_node` sets its message and RETURNS IMMEDIATELY, so no lane runs and it never competes with a computed answer. The only clarification that CAN compete is one raised by a lane that also produced a result -- exactly the spurious case.
Fix_Approach: Clarifications sit with the drafts, above the honest-decline fallback. They still reach the reader whenever nothing else answered, which is every case they were built for.
Verification: Probe 33/33 with the deliberate case answering rather than asking.

Title: The admission gate offered the reader the floor they had just named
Description: 'Which space on Floor 3 ...' answered 'Which floor did you mean? I know: Floor0, Floor1, Floor2, Floor3, Floor4, Floor5'. The log said only 'asking ONE question (slot=floor)' and DROPPED the reason, which carries the value that failed. Once the reason was logged it read 'unknown floor None': the CQ-IR compile emitted an ON_FLOOR qualifier -- it knew a floor was named -- with the literal string 'None' as the anchor. Separately, `_norm_floor` accepted only 'Floor 3', '3' and 'floor3', so 'Level 3', '3rd floor' and 'third floor' -- all spellings an LLM compile produces for the SAME question -- failed too (the BUG-184 shape, in a new place).
Root_Cause: Two independent faults reaching the same symptom, and the diagnostic that would separate them was being discarded one line before it was needed.
Fix_Approach: THREE parts. (1) The clarify log carries the reason. (2) `_norm_floor` reduces both sides to a STOREY NUMBER, so any spelling resolves while a floor the building lacks still clarifies -- and nothing assumes what a floor is called. (3) A null-ish anchor is recovered from `cqir.raw_query` against the building's own floor list: the compiler is one source, the question is the authoritative one. Recovery runs ONLY when the anchor is blank, so a compiled anchor that DISAGREES with the question still surfaces; and a room number like 3.10 is not read as a floor.
Verification: Probe 33/33, with no clarify question raised. 41 offline tests, including `Niveau-3` (a hyphen after a letter is a separator, not a minus sign -- my own normaliser read it as floor -3).

Title: A workflow was given less time than one LLM call inside it, so the report lane never finished
Description: Every `.env` in the repo carried LLM_TIMEOUT_S=180 and no WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_S, so the workflow deadline sat at its 120s default: one legal LLM call was allowed SIXTY SECONDS LONGER than the entire workflow containing it, and llm_manager retries each call up to MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS on top of that. The planner-driven report lane makes ~4 sequential calls and was killed at 120s on every attempt: 'Give me a report on energy use last week' at 15:25, 'on energy use yesterday' at 15:33 and 15:40, 'on the CO2 in room 5.01 yesterday' at 15:50 -- four questions, four kills, one per attempt. Narrowing from a building-week to one sensor and one day changed nothing, which is what proved the cost was the sequential calls and not the data.
Root_Cause: The two numbers were invisible to each other. WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_S is a Settings field in shared/config.py; LLM_TIMEOUT_S is read straight from os.environ in orchestrator/llm_manager.py and is not a Settings field at all. Nothing in the codebase ever printed them side by side, so no reviewer reading either file alone would see it and no test could fail -- the defect lived entirely in the gap between two configuration mechanisms. It surfaced only as a DEGRADED turn, which reads as an LLM problem, so every earlier look blamed the model.
Fix_Approach: WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_S now DERIVES from LLM_TIMEOUT_S when unset (0), at two full-length calls plus overhead -- 420s at the current 180s. Deriving four calls' worth was rejected: at LLM_TIMEOUT_S=180 that is a twelve-minute ceiling before a genuinely stuck request is reported, a worse deadline than the broken one. This bounds a HANG; it is not a budget for the slow path. An explicit value is KEPT rather than overruled -- a deployment may want to shed slow requests -- but an explicit value at or below LLM_TIMEOUT_S is warned about, naming BOTH numbers, since never seeing them together was the whole defect.
Verification: Live: `settings.WORKFLOW_TIMEOUT_S` reads 420 in the container from an unset value that previously meant 120. The report lane then completes instead of being killed. 8 offline tests including the exact live configuration (LLM 180 / workflow unset), a garbled LLM_TIMEOUT_S, and that a fast deployment is not pushed below the old 120s floor.

Title: The SQL prompt named every sensor in the building, so the model returned nothing and a data-free report went out
Description: `SchemaInfo.as_prompt_text` listed every column of every table. `sensor_data` is a WIDE table with one column per sensor -- 704 of them -- so the prompt reached 45,573 characters against OLLAMA_NUM_CTX=16384 and the model returned an EMPTY COMPLETION on all 3 attempts. Read the three log lines together: 'LLM returned an empty completion (prompt was 45573 chars)', 'SQL generation error: ... empty completion', then 'Report generated: 1360 chars'. SQL generation failed outright and a 1,360-character report was produced anyway, with no data behind it. The turn came back looking like an answer.
Root_Cause: The prompt grew with the BUILDING rather than with the question, and the caller knew which columns it wanted the whole time -- `group_uuids`, a handful -- and never said. Naming every column in the database costs ~34,203 characters before any of the prompt's own text. This is not a one-building problem: a larger building is strictly worse, and this one stops at 704 columns only because InnoDB stops at 1,017. Raising the context window (what BUG-188 did) moves the cliff without removing it.
Fix_Approach: `as_prompt_text(keep_columns)` lists a table in full while it is within a 60-column budget, and above that names only the columns the caller intends to query plus the timestamp column. Threaded through `get_schema_text(storage_uri, keep_columns)` and `prompt_text_for()`; the structured path passes `group_uuids`, and the fallback path passes what the turn has resolved via `contributing_uuids`. A caller that names nothing still gets a SAMPLE of the shape, because a wide table is unusable if the model cannot see that sensor identifiers appear as column names. The truncation is STATED with a count and the words 'NOT evidence that the data is missing' -- silence about a column must never become BUG-192's shape, a model denying a sensor class exists by reasoning from its window instead of a count.
Verification: LIVE VERIFIED 2026-09-10 (V12-02); the earlier note that this still needed the probe is discharged. Q 'Give me a report on the CO2 in room 5.01 yesterday.' -> a full report WITH data (avg 745.338 ppm, min 477, max 1030, latest 1015), 192.2s, intent=report. The 45,573-char / 704-column prompt no longer starves the model. BUG-479's row-cap disclosure is live in the same answer: '1,000 analyzed readings ... the overall period contains more readings than captured in this analysis'. Offline: 7 tests including the live shape (704 columns, 16k context) and a scaling check that 70 vs 7,000 sensors produce the same prompt. Two new defects were found IN this answer and are logged separately as BUG-506, which is where they are tracked rather than here.

Title: A report explained its own empty result as a monitoring gap and recommended installing a sensor
Description: 'Give me a report on the CO2 in room 5.01 yesterday.' returned: 'No CO2 sensor was active or present in Room 5.01', 'Data Void: a critical monitoring gap', 'Potential System Failure', 'Verify Sensor Installation', 'Deploy a secondary CO2 monitoring device'. That room's CO2 is recorded 77,088 times a day. The verifier had already scored the turn grounded=False, confidence=0.20, source=none, sql_rows=0 and the report went out regardless.
Root_Cause: `_narrate` was handed `data_points: 0` and a prompt demanding 'Recommendations (2-3 actionable items)'. Nothing told it that zero rows means the RETRIEVAL failed rather than that the sensor is absent, so it inferred a cause and acted on it. Worse than an ordinary wrong answer because it READS as honesty: 'no data was recorded' is the shape of this project's honest no-data answer, so it passes the referent gate, the leak grader and a reader's eye.
Fix_Approach: An empty retrieval is STATED and NOT EXPLAINED, by a deterministic `_no_data_narrative` reached BEFORE `_narrate` -- telling a model not to speculate is a request, not calling it is a guarantee. The text says explicitly that this is about the query and not the building, and that it does not mean the sensor is missing.
Verification: Live re-ask returns the honest text with no diagnosis. 16 offline tests, one per claim the live answer made.

Title: _standardize_results had no return statement, so every planned query lost its SPARQL results
Description: Annotated `-> Dict[str, Any]`. It builds the dict, fills it from the bindings, and falls off the end -- returning None on every call, on every path, since it was written. The planner's `_extract_uuids`, `_extract_storage_map` and `_extract_sensor_metadata` therefore returned empty on every multi-step plan this system has ever run.
Root_Cause: Silent because every consumer reads it defensively: `.get('standardized', {})` then `isinstance(std, dict)`, which is False for None, yielding []. A total failure of the data handoff was indistinguishable from 'this question had no sensors' -- a real and common case. Silence was already a legal answer. The SPARQL was correct throughout: it resolved the zone, picked brick:CO2_Level_Sensor from the HBCO concept, ran, and logged results=1. The one row it found was handed to a function that dropped it.
Fix_Approach: Added the return, after the try/except so both paths return. An AST scan of all 1,276 annotated functions in orchestrator/ found no other instance, and that scan is now a test so the class cannot come back.
Verification: Live: the planner now logs 'Fetching data for 1 UUIDs from storage: database1' and 'Query returned 1000 rows' where it previously let the LLM guess `WHERE uuid = '5.01'`. 6 offline tests including the class-wide AST guard.

Title: The report agent read the SQL and SPARQL results one level too shallow, so no report ever saw its data
Description: `_build_sections` read `sensor_data.get('data')` and `metadata.get('sensors')`. Both callers -- the planner's `_run_report` and the workflow's report node -- pass the WHOLE `sql_result` and `sparql_result`, which carry their rows at ['results']['data'] and ['standardized']['results'] respectively. So `data_points` and `sensor_count` were 0 on every report ever generated. Measured: the planner logged 'Query returned 1000 rows' and the report built from them said no data was retrieved.
Root_Cause: A shape mismatch between producer and consumer, silently yielding empty -- the same class as BUG-476, one lane over.
Fix_Approach: `_records_from` / `_sensors_from` accept both the wrapped and unwrapped shapes. Reading both rather than picking one, because narrowing to a single accepted shape is how a working caller gets broken silently, which is this bug.
Verification: Live: the report now carries real figures (count 1000, min 817, max 1112, avg 995.132), and the narration matches the computed sections exactly. 21 offline tests.

Title: A planned report about a named day described a different period, with real figures
Description: `PlannerAgent._run_sql` called `fetch_data_for_uuids(uuids, query, storage_map)` and passed neither start_date nor end_date, so the SQL lane fell back to its default window: `datetime >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) ORDER BY datetime DESC LIMIT 1000`, whose sample row was timestamped the afternoon the question was asked. The report was headed 'Room 5.01 - Yesterday' and described today: avg 993.81 ppm against yesterday's true 781.01, and a maximum of 1,112 above yesterday's actual 1,102.
Root_Cause: The main workflow's SQL lane has always passed these dates; only the planner-driven lane dropped them. So the defect appeared exactly on multi-step questions -- reports, comparisons, trends -- which are the ones where the period matters most. Harder to catch than a fabrication: every figure is real and measured, they are internally consistent, and the header names the right day.
Fix_Approach: `_run_sql` forwards start_date, end_date and sensor_metadata from the turn. A test pins that the two lanes forward the same arguments so they cannot drift apart again.
Verification: Live: the generated SQL now bounds the window to the requested period. 5 offline tests.

Title: A report states the row LIMIT as the number of readings the building recorded
Description: The report says 'Room 5.01 recorded 1,000 CO2 sensor readings yesterday'. 1,000 is the query's LIMIT; the true count in the window queried was 2,770. The statistics are correctly computed over the 1,000 rows fetched, but that sentence is a claim about the BUILDING and it is false. Same family as 'a cap on an exhaustive query does not fail; it under-reports', now surfacing in prose.
Root_Cause: `overview.data_points` is the length of the fetched list, and the narration has no way to know a cap was applied, so it reads the number as a fact about the period.
Fix_Approach: The truncation travels WITH the number. The fetch names its cap once (_row_limit), sets rows_capped when any storage group comes back exactly full, and carries rows_capped/row_limit out on the result. The report reads that flag rather than re-deriving it -- comparing len(rows) to a literal 1000 in a second file is how a cap and its detector drift apart -- and sets data_points_are_complete plus a note saying the figure is what was ANALYSED and the true count is higher. The narration prompt states the rule explicitly and names the wrong verb, because a note buried in serialised JSON competes with an instruction that says be specific. An absent flag means NOT capped: claiming a truncation that did not happen is its own false statement.
Verification: Live 2026-09-08: the report now reads '1,000 analyzed readings' and 'These statistics represent a slice of the full dataset; the complete period contains additional readings beyond the analyzed sample.' It previously said the room 'recorded 1,000 CO2 sensor readings yesterday' against a true 2,770. 10 offline tests.

Title: 'yesterday' resolves to a rolling 24 hours ending now, not the calendar day
Description: After BUG-478, the same question produced `datetime >= '2026-09-06 17:16:39' AND datetime <= '2026-09-07 17:16:39'` -- a 24-hour lookback ending at the moment of asking, half of which is TODAY. A report headed 'Yesterday' that covers this afternoon is misleading even though every figure in it is real.
Root_Cause: The time-range resolver treats a named day as a duration rather than as calendar bounds.
Fix_Approach: A named calendar day resolves to that day LOCAL midnight-to-midnight, via calendar_day_bounds(), applied AFTER the compiled range and overriding it -- the question is the authoritative source and the compile is one reading of it, the same lesson as recovering a floor from the raw query (BUG-472). The end is 23:59:59 rather than the next midnight because the SQL builders emit <=. Scope is deliberately narrow: only words whose day boundaries are not in dispute. last night spans two dates, this morning is a part-day, the weekend is two days and which two depends on where you are -- all return None and the compiled range stands, because a wrong window is not better than none. The timezone comes from the building context, never a literal: a day is the occupants Tuesday, not UTCs.
Verification: Live 2026-09-08: the generated SQL bounds the window to '2026-09-07 00:00:00' .. '2026-09-07 23:59:59' -- a whole calendar day -- and the log records the override correcting a rolling one: 'calendar day named in the question - window set to ... (was 2026-09-07 02:22:4x)'. 24 offline tests.

Title: Every concept-triggered ECA rule was dark: a setting that never existed, then a predicate the graph does not carry
Description: TWO faults in series, the second hidden by the first. (1) `_uuid_for_class` opened with `settings.ONTOLOGY_NAMESPACE`, which Settings has never had. The AttributeError was raised outside that method's own try, so it surfaced through `_resolve_uuid`'s broad except as '[rules_engine] concept resolve failed for temperature_reading / crowded / busyness / lift_status', once per rule per cycle. (2) With the namespace fixed the error stopped and the FAILURE did not: every concept still resolved to None, now silently, because the query joined on `brick:hasExternalReference` -- 2 triples in the whole repository, both from the Brick vocabulary -- instead of `ref:hasExternalReference`, which has 2,860. The join never matched a real sensor for ANY class, including brick:Temperature_Sensor, of which this building has 288.
Root_Cause: Two things hid it, neither of them a missing test. The MESSAGE named the wrong component: 'concept resolve failed for temperature_reading' reads as a missing lay-term mapping, fixed in hbco_mappings.ttl, while the actual fault was a programming error two calls away in a method the message never mentions. And a rule that never fires is indistinguishable from a rule whose condition is not met -- the ECA engine's normal state IS silence, so total failure and correct operation produce identical output. V10 recorded the engine as newly live; it was live and inert.
Fix_Approach: The namespace resolves from the engine's OWN _building_id via resolve_building_context (RulesEngine is per building; a background loop has no request context), falling back to BUILDING_NAMESPACE. The query joins on ref:hasExternalReference, follows rdfs:subClassOf* so a building that types its points more specifically still matches, and carries ORDER BY so which point a rule watches does not vary between restarts. The warning now names the rule, the exception TYPE, and the consequence ('this rule cannot fire') instead of blaming the concept resolver.
Verification: Live, in the container: namespace resolves to the building's own; busyness -> d7baf689... (11,812 rows) and temperature_reading -> 89d4f4fe... (62,085 rows), both None before. 11 rules loaded, zero ONTOLOGY_NAMESPACE errors in the logs. 13 offline tests. 'damp' still resolves to nothing and that is correct -- no HBCO mapping exists for it, which is the case the warning is for.

Title: A concept-triggered rule watches one arbitrary point and reads as if it covers the building
Description: `_uuid_for_class` returns a single UUID, so a rule written as 'alert when temperature_reading > 26' binds to ONE of the 288 temperature sensors in this building. Which one is invisible from the rule definition, and nothing in the rule's name, its YAML, or any alert it raises says the scope is one point.
Root_Cause: The concept path was built to answer 'give me a sensor for this concept' when the useful question is 'give me the sensors'. It was never noticed because the whole path returned None until BUG-481 was fixed -- the arbitrariness had no opportunity to mislead anyone.
Fix_Approach: PARTIALLY fixed. The engine now considers up to CLASS_CANDIDATES points of the class and keeps the first that actually REPORTS A VALUE, instead of taking whichever IRI sorted first. That mattered immediately: 'damp' had bound to RH_Sensor_F0, which holds zero rows, for a rule named humidity_damp_floor3 -- it bound and still could not fire, with nothing logging a problem. The chosen point is now named in the log at the moment the choice is made, with 'this rule watches THIS point only'. STILL OPEN: a concept trigger evaluates ONE point rather than all matching ones, and nothing lets a rule state a scope -- temperature_reading currently binds to the outside weather feed, which is a legal choice and probably not the intended one.
Verification: PARTIALLY SUPERSEDED 2026-09-17 by TODO-528. A rule can now be scoped to a floor or space and report its own coverage -- engine.coverage(rule_id) records concept, scope, place, in_scope (points located there), watched (uuids actually evaluated), their IRIs, and whether the query was truncated -- so 'a rule watches ONE point of however many carry the class' is no longer true for a scoped rule, and a scoped rule now states three distinct absences instead of falling back: no point of the class is in the place ('it is NOT falling back to a point elsewhere in the building'); points are there but none is reporting; or the query hit its limit and coverage is a prefix rather than the set. || THE DOOR IS STILL OPEN ON THE UNSCOPED PATH and that is now BUG-644: _uuids_for_class has LIMIT 10 and no DISTINCT while a bldg1 point satisfies a/rdfs:subClassOf* by ~3 paths, so an unscoped scope: all rule can be watching as few as ~3 distinct points while claiming the whole class. Not fixed here because changing it changes what existing unscoped rules watch. || PRIOR: V12-20 2026-09-12: the rule now DECLARES its scope instead of the engine guessing. `scope: all` evaluates every matching point; `scope: first_reporting` watches one and says so; neither declared means the rule does not load. tests/test_eca_fixtures.py -- 19 tests. LIVE RE-ASK OWED: confirm on a live cycle that a scope:all rule reports every breaching point and that the shipped first_reporting rule still logs which point it chose. || Live poll cycle: damp -> RH_Sensor_F0, crowded/busyness -> IntrusionDetector_Floor0_A, temperature_reading -> feed_outside_weather, each logged with its candidate count. lift_status honestly reports that no Fault_Sensor is reporting.

Title: The lay term 'damp' has no HBCO mapping, so a shipped rule can never bind
Description: `humidity_damp_floor3` in input/rules.yaml triggers on the concept 'damp'. `concept_resolver.resolve('damp')` returns no match, so the rule resolves to no sensor. Unlike BUG-481 this is a genuine data gap and the warning now reports it correctly -- but a rule shipped in the building's own config that can never fire is still a defect.
Root_Cause: No hbco:Concept carries 'damp' as a layTerm; humidity concepts exist under other terms.
Fix_Approach: Added 'damp' as a layTerm on hbco:too_humid in ontology/hbco_mappings.ttl. Only the two-word 'damp feeling' was present, so resolve('damp') matched nothing. TTL-first per contract rule 2, and in the CORE mapping rather than a per-building overlay because it is the ordinary English word for what a humidity sensor reports.
Verification: Live: ttl_uploader re-uploaded hbco_mappings.ttl on restart and humidity_damp_floor3 now binds to a reporting point. It bound to a DEAD one first, which is what exposed BUG-482 and the value-fetcher defect below.

Title: Probe expectations that move with the calendar must be computed, not written down
Description: 'How many sensors are overdue for calibration?' was pinned at 201, itself a re-baseline from 194, and failed on 2026-09-08 because the true answer had become 206: ontosage:calibrationDueOn dates pass as real time advances, so five more sensors fell overdue and the system reported them correctly. Nothing was broken except the expectation.
Root_Cause: A frozen number for a quantity that moves with the calendar is a scheduled false alarm: it decays quietly and fires on a day nobody chose -- here, the morning before a planned test.
Fix_Approach: expect_sparql added to the probe (the expectation is computed from the graph at run time), and the AUDIT of the other 49 cases is DONE -- measured against the graph, not reasoned about. Ten cases expect a bare number; every one except calibration is a stored literal. recoveryMinutes looked like the dangerous one, since "how long to recover after a full class" reads as computed from live readings and the publisher adds a row every 30s -- it is ontosage:recoveryMinutes 26.0 in the graph. The permit count is recordStatus "open", a status literal and not a date comparison. So calibration was the only expectation compared against NOW(). A guard test now fails any future case whose question asks what is overdue/due/expired while freezing a number, and checks that a graph query which cannot run produces a FAILING expectation rather than a skipped one.
Verification: FIRST CONFIRMED INSTANCE FOUND 2026-09-17, and it had already gone stale: the w0 lift case asserted expect_any ['not operational', 'out of service']. asset_state_service renders 'out of service since' ONLY while a live outage EPISODE exists and 'last checked' otherwise, so that pair silently required the building to be broken at the moment of the run. It passed for weeks and stopped passing when the episode ended. WORSE, IT WAS INVISIBLE: the probe's `why` is an elif chain reporting only the FIRST failing category, so a simultaneous 'missing' hid it completely -- a decayed marker can therefore sit undetected behind any other failure in the same case. Replaced with the two values the template can actually render, so the assertion holds in either state. The remaining 49 cases are still unaudited. || PRIOR: 4 offline guard tests; metrology group 3/3 with the computed expectation; full probe 50/50.

Title: The ECA value fetcher named one table in one database, so every narrow-store rule was blind
Description: _default_value_fetcher ran SELECT `<uuid>` FROM sensordb.sensor_data ... -- a database AND table literal in a core service. This building keeps occupancy, humidity, CO2 and the rest in narrow per-modality tables, so every point living there returned no value and the ECA engine could only ever have fired on wide-table sensors. Measured: busyness resolves to a point with 11,812 rows and the fetcher returned None for it.
Root_Cause: The fetcher constructed a bare MySQLAdapter() per call instead of routing through the adapter registry, bypassing ref:storedAt entirely -- so it could not have found a narrow table even in principle. Invisible because a rule that never fires looks exactly like a rule whose condition is not met.
Fix_Approach: Routes by ref:storedAt through adapter_registry and asks the adapter to build its own query, which is how every other lane does it and what makes a new backend a new adapter. The wide-table fallback discovers its table from the adapter schema by finding the one carrying the uuid as a COLUMN, rather than naming it. _uuids_for_class now selects ?storage, and a rule naming a uuid directly gets a one-off lookup -- without that, every candidate had an empty storage key and fell back to the default adapter, which is the same bug wearing the fix.
Verification: Live in the container with the registry initialised: wide-table point -> 21.29, narrow-table point -> 2.0. Both None before. Real poll cycle now binds four concept rules to reporting points across both store shapes.

Title: The building was the one space the system could not be asked about, and asking produced a garbled false negative
Description: Three live failures on the most natural opening question anyone asks. "What is measured in this building?" and "What is monitored across the whole building?" both returned "**Which space did you mean?**" -- a clarify loop demanding a scope the question had already given. And "What can you measure in this building?" returned "**No -- in this building is not measured in this building.** There is no point of that kind located there, so any figure I gave you would be invented." Garbled, and a confident negative about a referent that does not exist.
Root_Cause: TWO faults meeting. (1) NAMED_QUANTITY_RE captured the words "in this building" as the QUANTITY: the group is non-greedy and the trailing \s*\? lookahead accepted a preposition phrase, so a verb followed straight by a preposition produced a quantity name out of the scope. (2) _observability_space recognised rooms and floors only -- the building, the OUTERMOST space and the one the question named, was the single space it could not resolve. So the scope was never missing; the resolver could not see it, and the lane asked the reader for what they had already supplied. That is the BUG-472 shape exactly.
Fix_Approach: A negative lookahead after the verb, so a preposition or scope word names no quantity. And an OPEN question with no resolvable space is now answered with the menu the lane can always produce -- the modalities the building declares, from load_modalities, under the building name resolved from building context rather than a literal. NARROWED to open questions on purpose: a SPECIFIC question about an unnamed room still clarifies, because there the answer genuinely varies space by space and asking is correct.
Verification: Live: all three now return "**Across Abacws Building I can measure:** air_quality, co2, ..." in 13-36s. Room-scoped questions unchanged -- "Can you measure noise in room 5.01?" -> "Yes ... and the sensor is reporting", "What is measured in room 5.01?" -> the room menu. 19 offline tests, including that real quantities (formaldehyde, radon, carbon monoxide) are still named.

Title: A Python tuple decided which record classes could be named as ABSENT, so declared classes were unaskable
Description: record_registry's own module docstring names this sin and the ABSENT path was still committing it. _ALL_CLASS_TERMS was seeded from _FALLBACK_RECORD_CLASSES, load_lay_terms asked the graph only about those names, and any class outside the tuple was dropped by `if local not in _ALL_CLASS_TERMS: continue`. Measured live: 40 record classes discovered, absent-vocabulary limited to the tuple. ontosage:AlarmEvent, AnomalyEvent and AccessEvent are declared, carry 8-10 lay terms each, are discovered, and hold no instances -- so none could be named as absent. 'Have there been any alarms this week?' matched neither a held class nor an absent one and fell to the document lane; 'Show me the anomaly events' matched PublicEvent, because 'events' is one of ITS lay terms.
Root_Cause: The held-class path was fixed for exactly this reason (discovery from the ontology) and the absent path was left behind. Two code paths, one lesson, applied once.
Fix_Approach: load_lay_terms builds its class list from _discover_record_classes(), UNIONED with the fallback rather than replacing it -- discovery can degrade on a graph hiccup and losing the vocabulary entirely would be worse than an over-broad one. The vocabulary is seeded BEFORE the skip check, so a discovered class is no longer dropped before its lay terms are read.
Verification: V12-02 LIVE RE-ASK 2026-09-10: REFUTED. Q 'Show me the anomaly events' -> intent=metadata, and the answer returned TWO REAL ROWS from the events register ('2 events not in the normal scheduled state': a moved postgraduate welcome and a cancelled estates forum) || VERIFIED LIVE 2026-09-17 against the running graph: the vocabulary is 43 DISCOVERED classes, not the 20-odd fallback tuple — 40 held by this building and 3 declared-but-absent (AccessEvent, AlarmEvent, AnomalyEvent). The absent path names them: 'show me the alarm log' -> AlarmEvent, 'which access events were recorded' -> AccessEvent, while 'when was the fire alarm last tested' and 'which work orders are open' both return None because those classes are HELD — the match-length tie-break keeping real answers.

Title: SustainabilityTarget held five instances and no class could reach it
Description: ontosage:SustainabilityTarget was declared as a bare owl:Class with no rdfs:subClassOf. Record discovery walks rdfs:subClassOf+ from Record and IntervalRecord, so it found every record class except this one -- while five instances sat in the graph carrying fourteen declared lay terms. 'What are our sustainability targets?' matched no held class and no absent one. Data present, question unanswerable, nothing logged.
Root_Cause: A class can be authored with a label, a comment, an example and lay terms and still be invisible, because the one triple discovery depends on is the one with no visible consequence when omitted.
Fix_Approach: Added rdfs:subClassOf ontosage:Record in the TBox (contract rule 2 -- extend the TTL, do not special-case in code). Record and not IntervalRecord: the instances carry recordStatus / recordOwner / recordVersion / recordId, which is a standing record rather than something with an interval lifecycle like a booking or an alarm. A guard test now PARSES the TBox and fails on any lay-termed class with no path to a discovery root.
Verification: Live after re-upload: SustainabilityTarget is discovered and HELD, and both 'What are our sustainability targets?' and 'What is our carbon reduction target?' resolve to it. The guard test caught a second suspected orphan (ServiceSchedule) which turned out to be a FALSE POSITIVE of my own regex -- it declares its parent on the following line -- so the guard now parses with rdflib instead of grepping.

Title: A held register matched by a generic shared word outranks an absent one matched by a specific phrase
Description: 'Show me the anomaly events.' scores PublicEvent as the HELD class, because 'events' is one of its lay terms, while AnomalyEvent -- named by the question almost exactly -- is merely reported as absent. The held-class short-circuit in dialogue_agent fires first, so the question is answered from the public-event register. This is the shape record_registry's docstring already warns about: 'a greedy lay-term match must not outrank a class the building demonstrably holds' -- stated for the opposite direction, and the converse is now the live failure.
Root_Cause: Held and absent are ranked independently and never compared. Specificity of the match is not part of the decision between them.
Fix_Approach: NOT FIXED, deliberately. It changes routing, and this project's rule is that a routing change is gated on the live regression probe -- which needs the local model, and the GPU is committed elsewhere. Landing it unverified is how BUG-431's first fix corrected one question and started answering another with the building-wide total. Do it with the probe green, one comparison, then re-run.

Title: AlarmEvent and AccessEvent lay terms miss the phrasings people actually use
Description: With the vocabulary fixed, 'Have there been any alarms this week?' still matches nothing: AlarmEvent declares 'alarm activation', 'alarm event', 'false alarm', 'alarm history' and 'when did the alarm sound' but no bare 'alarm'/'alarms'. 'Who accessed the server room?' misses AccessEvent for the same reason -- 'accessed' is not among its terms.
Root_Cause: Lay-term coverage is authored, and these were authored as compound phrases only.
Fix_Approach: TWO changes, in this order, because the second is unsafe without the first. (1) absent_record_class now compares MATCH LENGTH instead of returning the first absent class in dict order, and a HELD class wins ties -- a decline costs a real answer while a held class merely routes to data that exists, the same asymmetry _ALL_CLASS_TERMS already documents. (2) Bare and colloquial forms added to AlarmEv || COMPLETED 2026-09-17. Parts (1) and (2) were already in place — absent_record_class compares match length with held winning ties, and the bare 'alarm'/'alarms'/'accessed' terms are declared. The SUBSTANCE was still broken: the classifier called 'Have there been any alarms this week?' an `alert`, and the alert lane creates standing alerts, so it replied 'I haven't created an alert yet. I need what to measure ... and the value that should trigger it' — a configuration form in answer to a question about what occurred. New parse-stage rule `alarm_history_is_a_record` claims the PAST shape only, and fires only when STANDING_ALERT_RE does not, so the two opposites cannot both claim one question.
Verification: tests/test_an_alarm_that_happened_is_a_record.py (14 tests): six past-tense shapes leave the alert lane, five standing requests keep it, a non-alert intent is untouched, the rule's position is pinned, and the two patterns are asserted disjoint. Contract suite 175 green. LIVE 2026-09-17: 'Have there been any alarms this week?' -> "The building's events store doesn't record that. It holds room bookings, work orders, aggregate entrance counts and detected anomaly episodes", with three suggestions; 'Alert me when the CO2 in room 5.01 goes above 1000.' -> 'Alert created (ID: bdb23e0b)'. 'When was the fire alarm last tested?' still answers from the held FireSafetyAsset register, so the length tie-break holds.

Title: The readiness report described an empty building whenever it could not reach the stores
Description: check_onboarding.py wrapped adapter initialisation in `except Exception: pass`, reasoning that the registry is already initialised inside the app process. True there. Run on the HOST -- where database_registry.yaml carries container-internal hostnames -- initialisation fails, every time-series lookup returns nothing, and the report is emitted anyway. Measured on a healthy bldg1, the same minute: from the host 'history 0.0 days, events rows 0, adjacency 0, 4/11 unlocked'; inside the container 'history 8.0 days, events rows 98,139, adjacency 270, 10/11 unlocked'. The first printed, wrote itself to scripts/outputs/, and exited 0.
Root_Cause: A report about capability cannot tell an absent capability from an unreachable one, and this one resolved the ambiguity silently in the wrong direction. Anyone acting on it would open defects against a building that answers those questions.
Fix_Approach: It refuses. An init exception OR a registry that comes back with no adapters at all -- the same blindness by a quieter route -- prints why, says where to run it, quantifies what it would have got wrong (4/11 versus 10/11), and exits 2. The principle is already stated in certify_building.py: a run that cannot be trusted is better not started than explained away afterwards. The docstring no longer suggests the host as a place to run it, which is how this happened.
Verification: Host run now prints the refusal and exits 2. Container run still reports 10/11 with history 8.0 days, 98,139 events and 270 adjacency edges. 7 offline tests.

Title: Five of six services reaching the Docker host never declared the host gateway, so Linux loses MySQL and Ollama
Description: Six services in every compose file name host.docker.internal; exactly one (adminer) declared `extra_hosts: host.docker.internal:host-gateway`. Docker Desktop resolves that name whether or not it is declared, so on the development machine this has always worked. On Linux it does not resolve at all -- and the orchestrator uses it for BOTH MySQL and Ollama. A fresh clone on a Linux host boots, passes every container health check, and cannot answer one question about sensor data, with nothing in the logs naming the cause.
Root_Cause: A prerequisite that is invisible on the machine it was developed on. The mapping was added to the one service where its absence was once noticed, and the other five were never revisited.
Fix_Approach: Declared on every service that names the host, in all four compose files (20 insertions). A no-op on Docker Desktop, which already provides it. A guard test fails on any service that reaches the host without declaring it, and also on a declaration that is not needed -- noise in a compose file is how the next reader stops believing it.
Verification: `docker compose config` valid on all four files; stack brought up with the change and /health reports mysql ok across 20 backends. 16 offline tests over every compose file present.

Title: .env.example pointed a fresh clone at a MySQL service that is commented out, and the wrong database
Description: The example carried MYSQL_HOST=mysql and MYSQL_DATABASE=abacws. There is no mysql service -- the block in docker-compose.yml is commented out -- and the live database is sensordb; abacws is the legacy name data/mysql-init/init.sql still creates. A clone copying this file boots green and fails every sensor question.
Root_Cause: MySQL became a HOST prerequisite when the container was disabled, and the example was never moved with it. Nothing checks the example against reality, only against the live .env -- which is gitignored, so the drift was invisible.
Fix_Approach: The block now states the prerequisite in the first line, gives the three steps before starting the stack, names the containerised alternative, and carries the values that actually work (host.docker.internal / ontosage / sensordb).
Verification: The existing .env-versus-example guard still passes (0 undocumented live settings).

Title: 79 settings the code reads are absent from .env.example
Description: 54 Settings fields and 25 raw os.environ names appear in neither .env nor .env.example -- including DELIBERATE_CLARIFY_OFF, one of the two gating variables W4-1 records as existing in no Settings and no .env. Every one has a usable default, so none blocks a fresh clone; they are undiscoverable rather than broken.
Root_Cause: The existing guard checks .env against the example, and these are in neither.
Fix_Approach: Re-measured 2026-09-17 before doing anything, and the number had moved: 0 of the 122 Settings fields were undocumented (they had been added since), leaving 26 raw os.environ names. The row's own judgement was kept — document what changes BEHAVIOUR, leave internal tuning to ONTOSAGE.md — so 22 were added to .env.example with their REAL defaults and a line on what each one does: agent and cross-session memory, language detection, the ARBITER compile cache, the whole LLM retry policy including LLM_RUNNER_RESTART_WAIT_S, the local model runtime, the response cache, rate limits, translation providers, the ontology-detector threshold and the plugin list.
Verification: tests/test_a_behaviour_flag_is_discoverable.py (4 tests): every Settings field documented, every behaviour flag documented, the exclusion list capped at 8 and each entry asserted to be actually read somewhere, and four load-bearing defaults checked against the values the code uses — a worked example that lies is worse than no example. Undocumented names: 79 claimed -> 4 remaining, and those four are build-time or internal (BUILD_SHA, BUILD_TIME, DEFAULT_BUILDING_ID, DOCS_OUTPUT_DIR).

Title: The deliberative plan trace reported a constant six-step list for every answer
Description: build_plan_trace returned the same hardcoded list -- compile_cqir, admission_gate, enumerate_candidates, fetch_aggregate, score, dossier_guard -- for every deliberative answer, regardless of what ran. Two executor stages are CONDITIONAL and appeared in it never: plan_executor times events_ms only when event checks apply and forecast_ms only when the top-K are forecast, so a run that forecast was indistinguishable from one that did not. And a plan parked at the admission gate never reaches the executor at all, yet still reported 'score' and 'dossier_guard' as done.
Root_Cause: The trace was written from the code's shape rather than from the request's. It sits in the response beside plan_hash and plan_fingerprint, which ARE evidence, so a constant list borrows their credibility and answers nothing.
Fix_Approach: Derived from the dossier's timings_ms, which the executor writes per stage as it runs. The two pre-executor stages stay unconditional because the dossier is built from their output, and dossier_guard is appended because the dict being read IS the dossier. A test pins the stage table against the timing keys plan_executor actually writes -- a rename there would otherwise drop a stage from every trace with nothing failing.
Verification: 10 offline tests covering a plain run, a forecasting run, an event-checking run, a plan parked at admission, and scrambled timing order.

Title: The complete technical reference never mentioned the deliberation lane
Description: ONTOSAGE.md contained ZERO mentions of ARBITER, CQ-IR, the dossier, plan_fingerprint or SATURATE, while V4-T26 was marked done and the lane answers the project's most-cited example question. DELIBERATE_CLARIFY_OFF -- an ablation switch that stops the lane asking its one clarifying question -- existed in the code and in no Settings, no .env and no .env.example.
Root_Cause: The lane was built as an improvement plan and never folded into the reference.
Fix_Approach: New section 5.7 stating the design claim first (the LLM's only generative role is words to symbols; every number after that is code), the stage-by-stage flow, the plan_fingerprint versus plan_hash distinction WITH the reason plan_hash differs between runs, SATURATE, and the env var in a table. DELIBERATE_CLARIFY_OFF documented in .env.example with the warning that an unasked question becomes an undeclared guess.
Verification: 4 offline tests, including that the reference states the design CLAIM and not merely the parts list, and that it still distinguishes the two hashes.

Title: The building declares its lifts under two type systems, and the answer only counts one of them
Description: CORRECTED 2026-09-10, same day, after reading the code instead of inferring from a SPARQL result. FIRST VERSION of this row claimed 'the denominator counts only assets carrying a status record'. That was wrong. asset_state_service._status_query builds '?asset a ontosage:{class}' and is called with 'Lift', so the lane counts ontosage:Lift - and exactly one subject, bldg:Lift_Main, carries that type. '1 of 1 lift(s) are not operational' is therefore CORRECT for what the lane asks. WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG: the same building separately declares THREE brick:Elevator - Lift_1 'Passenger Lift 1' and Lift_2 'Passenger Lift 2 / Goods Lift' in bldg1_abacws_metadata.ttl, and LIFT-01 'Main Passenger Lift' in equipment_linkage.ttl, the last commented 'Single passenger lift serving all 6 floors'. The lane never sees them. So a user asking 'is the lift working?' is told about one lift while the graph describes four entities across three files under two incompatible typings, and the answer gives no hint that the other declarations exist.
Root_Cause: Two parallel vocabularies for the same real assets. bldg1_lifts.ttl was added to fix BUG-438 - bldg:Lift_Main was named by a status record and a published accessibility survey but had no type triple, so the lane found nothing and answered 'this building has no lifts recorded in its model'. Typing it || THE DATA QUESTION IS SETTLED (building owner, 2026-09-17): there are TWO real lifts, one at each side — bldg:Lift_1 and bldg:Lift_2, both already declared and typed brick:Elevator in bldg1_abacws_metadata.ttl. bldg:Lift_Main was a THIRD name for the same fabric, invented in bldg1_lifts.ttl so the status lane had a subject of type ontosage:Lift to match. A vocabulary added to satisfy a query became a wrong count: 'are the lifts working?' answered '1 of 1' about a building with two.
Fix_Approach: The two REAL assets now carry ontosage:Lift additively (they keep brick:Elevator, which is what Brick-aware readers look for) and the published accessibility description moves onto Lift_1 — the lift that survey describes, 'left from the front entrance'. Lift_2 gets its own entry as the opposite-side goods lift. Lift_Main is gone as an asset; the knowledge topic that referenced it now points at Lift_1, and the single status record became one per real lift. No generator change was needed: provision_synthetic_sources.py discovers lifts by `?s a ontosage:Lift`, so it will now produce a status for each.
Verification: SECOND DUPLICATE FOUND AND RETIRED 2026-09-17, after the first fix was already verified live. Retiring bldg:Lift_Main left bldg:LIFT-01 standing in input/equipment_linkage.ttl -- 'a brick:Elevator' labelled 'Main Passenger Lift' with the comment 'SINGLE passenger lift serving all 6 floors', which the owner's correction makes false -- so the graph still answered brick:Elevator with THREE subjects for a two-lift building, and it owned the lift vibration monitor. Found only because the regression probe's lift case failed on that subject's label, which is the probe doing exactly its job. Its real facts are kept and moved onto Lift_1 (the service date, the location, the vibration point); the duplicate subject is gone. owl:sameAs was deliberately NOT used: it leaves two subjects in every COUNT that does not reason over sameAs, and the count is the thing that was wrong. VERIFIED after re-upload: brick:Elevator now returns exactly Lift_1 and Lift_2, and 'Is the lift working?' answers 'All 2 lift(s) are operational (last checked 11 days ago)' identically on BOTH /chat (7.6 s) and /v1 (13.6 s). THE PROBE CASE WAS REWRITTEN, NOT LOOSENED: it now asserts the count ('2 lift') AND that the answer discloses the basis of that count -- which is what the case's own why-field had asked for in advance -- and forbids both the retired name and the old wrong count. It asserts strictly more than it dropped. || PRIOR: VERIFIED LIVE 2026-09-17 04:57 after restart + resp_cache flush. GraphDB now answers ontosage:Lift with exactly Lift_1 and Lift_2, one status record each (status_lift_0 / status_lift_1); Lift_Main is gone from the named graph because ttl_uploader PUTs the context rather than adding to it. 'Are the lifts working?' -> 'All 2 lift(s) are operational (last checked 11 days ago)' in 15.0 s, with the staleness stated rather than hidden. The count is now the building's own - it read 1 of 1 for a building with two.
Refs: orchestrator/services/asset_state_service.py:261,657; bldg1/bldg1_lifts.ttl; bldg1/bldg1_abacws_metadata.ttl; bldg1/equipment_linkage.ttl; BUG-438; V12-09; scripts/regression_cases.json (group w0)

Title: A response-cache entry outlived the code that produced it: a dishonest answer served after the guard held
Description: Corrected 2026-09-09, same day, after four more measurements. The FIRST version of this row claimed the W0 meta-answer guard had regressed, on ONE observation: 'Which rooms are stuffy right now?' returned the pivot prose and a 100-row 'Rooms with active sensors' table. That observation came back in 0.9 s, which is a cache hit, not a generation. Re-measured four times with resp_cache flushed before each ask and the orchestrator restarted in between: four identical honest declines, 457 chars each, 21-51 s. THE GUARD HOLDS. What was actually demonstrated is different and still real: a dishonest answer sat in the response cache and was served while the running code would not have produced it.
Root_Cause: response_cache._partition() keys on building_id, role and user_id only - verified by reading it. There is no revision, image SHA, prompt version or policy version in the key. So an answer produced by any earlier revision stays servable for the full 1 h TTL after the fix that would have prevented it is deployed. CLAUDE.md already documents 'flush resp_cache after a code fix' under Debugging - that is an operational workaround standing in for a contract, and it only helps whoever remembers.
Fix_Approach: FIXED under V12-16. The cache partition now carries a REVISION component: `{building_id}|{role[:user_id]}|r{revision}`. Revision is BUILD_SHA where the image carries one; where it does not - and it does not here, `docker exec` reports BUILD_SHA=unknown - it is the process boot time, which is the honest proxy in this deployment because /app/orchestrator is BIND-MOUNTED and a `docker compose restart` is therefore itself a deployment: new source, same image. That is exactly the case that bit us. Deliberately a KEY COMPONENT rather than another flush. policy_admin.invalidate_policy_caches already flushes on a policy edit and is kept - editing a policy does not change the code revision, so the key alone would not catch it - but a flush is wrapped in try/except and logs a warning when the cache object is missing, so it fails OPEN. A key component fails CLOSED: a changed signature is a miss, with nothing for anyone to remember to do. Revision is placed LAST so `invalidate`'s partition-blind `{building_id}|*` sweep still reaches every partition. COST, stated rather than discovered: without BUILD_SHA every restart starts from a cold cache. A cold cache is cheap; an answer from code that no longer exists is not.
Verification: 10 tests in tests/test_the_cache_cannot_outlive_its_authorisation.py covering both halves of B12: a narrower identity MISSES rather than hits, two people in an individually-scoped role do not share a partition, two estate-wide managers deliberately do, an entry from another revision is unreachable, the revision is derived rather than hardcoded and is never the literal 'unknown', the partition-blind sweep still matches, and the policy-edit flush is still wired. Verified partitions by hand: bldg1|occupant:alice|rboot..., bldg1|occupant:bob|rboot..., bldg1|facility_manager|rboot... NOT verified live: no model this session, so no end-to-end demonstration that a pre-restart answer is unreachable after a restart. The key comparison is proved; the round trip is owed. || LIVE VERIFIED 2026-09-11, the full round trip and not just the key comparison. Pre-restart: the question cost 10.1 s then 0.8 s (a hit) under key 'resp_cache:exact:bldg1|admin:8dd001c8...'. The orchestrator was restarted and the SAME question asked again WITHOUT flushing: 20.2 s - it recomputed - then 0.8 s under the new key 'resp_cache:exact:bldg1|admin|rboot1789137906:8dd001c8...'. Both keys were visible in Redis side by side: the pre-restart entry still EXISTS and is simply unreachable, which is the designed behaviour. It expires on its own TTL.
Refs: orchestrator/services/response_cache.py:231 (_partition); V12-16; CLAUDE.md Debugging 'Stale answers after a code fix'; docs/V10_LIVE_VERIFICATION.md; orchestrator/services/response_cache.py REVISION/_partition; tests/test_the_cache_cannot_outlive_its_authorisation.py; V12-16

Title: A question about a room that does not exist times out instead of declining
Description: 'What is the temperature in room 99.99?' returned TIMEOUT after 180.8 s with no intent recorded. The referent-existence gate exists precisely so an unknown room is refused immediately; instead the most cheaply answerable class of question is the most expensive, and the user sees a transport failure rather than 'that room is not in this building'.
Root_Cause: Not yet diagnosed. The gate either does not run before the data lanes on this phrasing, or runs after a full sensor resolution has already been attempted. Contrast: 'What is the radiation level in the atrium?' declines correctly in 59 s naming the measured quantities, so the MEASURAND branch of the gate works and the SPACE branch is the suspect.
Fix_Approach: Not yet fixed. Belongs with V12-05 (typed retrieval outcomes): a nonexistent referent is NOT_DECLARED and must terminate the turn, and with V12-19, under which a timeout is a typed outcome distinguishable from an answer. Do not fix by raising the timeout.
Verification: Observed live 2026-09-09 at 180.8 s. Deliberately NOT added as a probe case yet: a case that reliably times out costs 90-180 s on every run to re-report a known-open defect. It becomes a case under V12-05/V12-19 once the contract it should satisfy exists. || LIVE 2026-09-15 streamed first pass: "What is the temperature in room 99.99?" -> "'99.99' does not exist in this building" in 21 s (was TIMEOUT 180 s). Fixed by the referent gate work since; no code change in this batch.

Title: The same question varies 10.7s to past 121s, so a probe timeout can be latency rather than a defect
Description: 'Which teaching sessions are scheduled in Room 1.06?' timed out in the 2026-09-09 full probe run. Re-asked three times with the cache flushed before each: 10.7 s, 61.1 s, 13.3 s -- all status OK, all correct (23 sessions, three courses). Identical input, a spread of at least 10x and on one occasion past the 121 s client timeout.
