Title: coverage_audit enumerates 39,119 located points and took 13 minutes inside one turn
Description:
Regression-gate case 9/51, 'Where should I sit if I care most about low noise and second about ...', was recorded REGRESSED (answered -> empty) at exactly 420.0 s, which is the harness's own client timeout, not an answer. The orchestrator had not failed -- it was still working. Its log shows the cost:
    12:07:15  [coverage_audit] Discovered 234 spaces in <ns>
    12:20:30  [coverage_audit] Discovered 39119 located points
**13 minutes 15 seconds for one step of one turn**, enumerating 39,119 located points to answer a seat-choice question about noise and one other modality.
THE SAME CASE TOOK 28.1 s AT 08:52 TODAY, on the same build, in a gate run whose 51 cases had median 30.3 s and max 108.1 s and finished in 27.8 minutes. So this is not a fixed property of the lane; it is what the lane costs under conditions that have not been pinned down. Sibling case #12 went 48.3 s -> 3,412 s across the same interval (that one is BUG-1191, a different mechanism).
NOT CLAIMED: that this is a regression from today's changes. Today's ontology change REMOVED 71 timeseries references, which cannot enlarge a point enumeration, and the earlier run's own numbers show the lane can do this work in seconds. What IS established is that a single turn can spend a quarter of an hour in one audit step, and that no bound stops it.
Root_Cause:
Not diagnosed. The measured fact is the enumeration size (39,119 located points) and its duration; whether the cost is the SPARQL, the round trips, or the post-processing is unestablished. Two conditions differed from the fast run and BOTH are candidates rather than conclusions: `cache:sparql*` was flushed immediately before this run, so every query was cold, and the unit suite (13,228 tests) overlapped the gate's first cases. CAVEAT-467 records the same shape on floor comparison ('fetches about 1.8M rows', observed 63 s / 94 s / two timeouts), so a deliberation-family question exceeding its client's patience has precedent.
=== CORRECTED 2026-09-30: THIS IS A SYMPTOM OF BUG-1194, NOT A COST OF THE LANE ===
I recorded `coverage_audit` taking **13m15s to enumerate 39,119 located points** and wrote that 'a single turn can spend a quarter of an hour in one audit step'. Re-measured on a HEALTHY process, against the SAME graph and the SAME 39,119 points, with no code change:
    10.6 s,  14.7 s,  17.8 s
**Roughly 75x faster.** So the enumeration is not expensive; the process was. The row's own hedge -- 'the earlier run's numbers show the lane can do this work in seconds' -- was pointing at the right answer, and the 13m15s should never have been carried as a property of the lane.
**THE PRACTICAL LESSON IS ABOUT THE FIX I ALMOST SIZED.** This row proposed bounding the candidate set because 'a seat-choice question does not need all 39,119 located points'. A bound sized from 13m15s would have been sized from a degraded process, and would then have been credited with a 75x speedup that was really a restart. Re-read CAVEAT-942's 3,102 s and this row's own 420 s timeout the same way.
STATUS: the ENUMERATION SIZE is still worth questioning on design grounds -- 39,119 points for a seat-choice question is a lot of work to do at all -- but it is no longer a performance defect and must not be quoted as one. Severity P2 -> P3, and the fix approach is now 'measure on a healthy process first, and only then decide whether the scan needs bounding'.
Fix_Approach: Measure before optimising: time the audit's SPARQL directly against a warm and a cold cache, with nothing else on the host, and record both. If the enumeration is inherent, the lane needs a bounded candidate set rather than a faster full scan -- a seat-choice question does not need all 39,119 located points. NOT ATTEMPTED: changing a lane's query shape while its own measurement is unreliable is how a 'fix' gets credited with a speedup that was really a warm cache.
Refs: CAVEAT-467; BUG-1191; CAVEAT-500; BUG-1194 (the real cause)

Title: A turn outlives the client that abandoned it, so one slow question penalises the next
Description:
When the regression harness gave up on case 9 at its 420 s timeout, THE TURN KEPT RUNNING. Observed directly: the gate recorded the case at 12:09 and the orchestrator was still logging that turn's work at 12:22, thirteen minutes later (`coverage_audit ... 39119 located points`, then another adapter query at 12:22:00).
WHY THIS MATTERS FOR EVERY MEASUREMENT IN THIS REPO: the local runner is configured `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1`, so it serves one request at a time. Abandoned work is still work, and the next question queues behind it. A harness that times out therefore CREATES the contention that slows the cases after it -- each timeout making the following case more likely to time out. A run degrading case by case can be that feedback loop rather than a defect in the cases.
CONSEQUENCE ACTED ON TODAY: the gate was STOPPED at 9 of 51 rather than run to completion, because under this effect its remaining verdicts would not be evidence. Its one REGRESSED verdict is a 420.0 s timeout, not a behavioural change, and must not be quoted as a regression.
Root_Cause:
Client-side abandonment does not cancel server-side work, and nothing downstream of the HTTP request is bounded (BUG-1191: even the configured 180 s LLM timeout did not fire). With a single-slot local runner, that turns one slow turn into a queue.
=== MECHANISM REFINED THE SAME HOUR, because my first wording overstated it ===
I wrote 'client-side abandonment does not cancel server-side work'. Too strong. The orchestrator DOES notice -- `starlette.requests.ClientDisconnect` was raised for this very turn. What it does not do is notice at the CLIENT'S READ TIMEOUT.
The sequence, measured:
    12:02:02  turn starts
    ~12:09    harness's 420 s read timeout expires; it records the case and moves on
    12:20:30  orchestrator STILL working (coverage_audit, 39,119 points)
    12:22:00  orchestrator still working (adapter query)
    ~12:25    I kill the harness process -> the SOCKET finally closes
    12:27:04  ClientDisconnect raised, turn unwinds
So the turn ran ~25 minutes, of which ~16 were after its client had stopped caring. A `requests` read timeout abandons the READ; it does not promptly close the connection, so the server has nothing to detect until the process exits. The practical consequence is unchanged and is what the row is for -- on a single-slot runner that work still holds the slot and the next case queues behind it -- but the fix is now better aimed: the server needs its own deadline, because relying on the client to signal is relying on something that can be sixteen minutes late.
Fix_Approach: Two independent halves. (a) Give the workflow a deadline that actually abandons its own work when the client has gone, so abandoned turns stop consuming the runner. (b) Until then, RUN THE GATE ALONE -- no unit suite, no agents, no hand questions -- and treat any run with concurrent load as unusable for latency AND, because of the queueing above, unreliable for verdicts too.

Title: A door whose label says open=1/closed=0 is typed a Position_Sensor and reads 54% -- and unlike BUG-1150 this one is live TODAY
Description: bldg:Door_Sensor_Main_Entrance carries rdfs:label 'Door Position Sensor - Main Entrance (open=1 / closed=0)'. Its publish-map entry is lo=0 hi=100 dec=0, value_col vib_mm_s, table equipment_data. MEASURED 2026-09-30 12:05 UTC, session pinned '+00:00': the last 6 hours hold 60 rows reading 46.0..61.0, mean 54.7, 15 distinct values. A reader asked whether the main entrance is open gets 54. The whole history is the same shape: 2026-07-08..08-21 reads 43.6..95.9 at a 15-minute step (the linker's `position` profile: base 50, swing 40, capped at 100), then a spike era to 752.811 on 08-22..08-25, then 0.48..0.82 under the gap backfill's vib_mm_s range, then 46..61 live. Four writers, four quantities, one series. FOUND while falsifying BUG-1150's root cause: the door was that row's second example, and it turns out to be a DIFFERENT defect with a different owner. P3 rather than P2: it is one point, it is a demo-extension point rather than one of the building's real sensors, and the number is at least dimensionally a percentage. It is still a figure a reader would take at face value.
Root_Cause: A TTL TYPING DEFECT, NOT A GENERATOR DEFECT, and that distinction is the point. The generator chain is behaving correctly at every step: the graph types this point brick:Position_Sensor; the ontology declares brick:Position_Sensor -> o:LinearPositionPercent, o:typicalMin 0, o:typicalMax 100, dec 0; generate_publish_map.py takes the band from that declaration, which is TTL-first and right; and sensor_signal fills 0..100 because 0..100 is what it was handed. The contradiction is between the point's TYPE and its own LABEL, and the label is not a thing any generator reads -- nor should it be, since reading a label to decide a quantity is the name-substring approach this cluster exists to avoid. WHY THE NEW GUARD CANNOT SEE IT: scripts/audit_status_point_bands.py fails a point the ontology declares a STATUS and generates wider than 0..1. brick:Position_Sensor is a brick:Sensor, so this point is outside the rule -- correctly, because brick:Contact_Sensor is also a Sensor and is legitimately 0/1 on 479 points here. No structural rule over the CURRENT typing can catch this; only fixing the typing can.
Fix_Approach: NOT DONE -- input/*.ttl is outside this agent's files. TWO TRIPLES, and both are needed or the point goes from wrong to invisible. (1) Type the point brick:Open_Close_Status instead of (or as well as) brick:Position_Sensor, in the TTL that authors it. Open_Close_Status IS a brick:Status, so the point then falls under the new audit's rule and a future regression is caught rather than argued about. (2) DECLARE A MEASURAND ON brick:Open_Close_Status. It has NONE today -- checked against the live graph: Occupancy_Status, Occupancy_Count_Sensor, Position_Sensor and Contact_Sensor all return a typicalMin/typicalMax pair and Open_Close_Status returns nothing. generate_publish_map.py reports-and-skips a class with no measurand, so doing (1) alone would drop the point out of the publish map entirely and it would simply stop being written. Declare o:BinaryState 0..1 dec=0, the same measurand brick:Occupancy_Status and brick:Contact_Sensor already use. THEN regenerate the publish map. ALSO WORTH A LOOK, not blocking: the entry routes to `equipment_data` with value_col `vib_mm_s`, so a door's readings sit in a column named for vibration. That is cosmetic against the quantity error but it is how the door ended up on the backfill's (0.1, 1.2, 2) range during one of its four eras. HISTORY: 12,879 rows on one uuid, four eras. Same re-seed decision as BUG-1150 and the same recommendation -- leave it, and let the band audit report the eras.
Verification: scratchpad/probe_1150a.py and probe_1150b.py against the live store, session pinned '+00:00' and printed: n=12,879, all-history range 0.0..752.811, last 6 h 46.0..61.0 mean 54.68 over 60 rows. Graph: `?p a ?c` returns Resource, Class, Entity, Point, Sensor, Position_Sensor, NamedIndividual -- no Status. Measurand query against repo `bldg`: Position_Sensor -> LinearPositionPercent 0..100 dec=0; Open_Close_Status -> (no rows). NOT FIXED, so nothing is claimed verified beyond the measurement.

Title: The linker picks a point's modality from an UNORDERED class list, so a point carrying two mapped classes gets whichever the store happened to emit first
Description: scripts/link_unlinked_sensors.py line 328 (as of 2026-09-30): `modality = next((cls_map[c] for c in classes if c in cls_map), None)`. `classes` comes from line 151, a GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?cn) in the SPARQL at lines 146-158. GROUP_CONCAT's order is not specified by SPARQL and GraphDB does not promise one, so for any point whose class set contains TWO classes that both appear in class_to_modality(), the modality -- and therefore the value PROFILE and the destination TABLE -- is whichever the store listed first. It can differ between runs, and between GraphDB versions, with no error and no log line. NO POINT IS CURRENTLY AFFECTED on bldg1, which is why this is a caveat and not a bug: the six Booking_Status points carry exactly one mapped class (Occupancy_Status), and Status/Point/Entity/Resource/Class/NamedIndividual are all absent from the map. But the collision is designed for rather than against -- config/saturation_modalities.yaml deliberately gives FIVE Brick classes to more than one modality, counted from the file: Contact_Sensor and Open_Close_Status to door_contact AND window_contact; Motion_Sensor to occupancy AND motion; Occupancy_Count_Sensor to occupancy AND parking_free; Water_Flow_Sensor to water_flow AND water_flow_rate. The config resolves those splits with `label_contains` / `label_excludes`, which this script does not read at all. A single additively-typed point turns a config-resolved split into a coin flip. THE SAME UNORDEREDNESS ALSO SITS IN class_to_modality() ITSELF, line 182: `out.setdefault(<class>, modality)` makes the FIRST modality in YAML order win a shared class. That one is at least deterministic per file, but it is deterministic for a reason nobody wrote down -- Contact_Sensor resolves to door_contact purely because door_contact is declared above window_contact.
Root_Cause: A one-of-many choice made by iteration order over a set the query did not order, combined with a reverse map that drops the disambiguators the forward config carries. Same family as lessons #155 (a ranking that ties falls back to alphabetical and nobody reads it as alphabetical): the answer is stable enough to look intended and arbitrary enough to change under you.
Fix_Approach: FOR THE OWNER OF link_unlinked_sensors.py -- NOT APPLIED, the file is outside this agent's set. Three changes, smallest first, and none of them a name list: (1) LINE 328. Replace the first-match `next(...)` with an explicit collection and a stated tie-break: gather `mods = sorted({cls_map[c] for c in classes if c in cls_map})`; if len(mods) == 1 use it; if len(mods) > 1 PRINT the point and its candidates and put it in `unmapped` rather than guessing. That converts a silent arbitrary pick into a visible gap, which is this repo's stated preference and is what the script already does for a point with no mapped class at all. (2) LINE 151. `GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?cn; separator=",")` gives no order. Either keep the concat and rely on (1) to refuse ambiguity, or order it -- but (1) is the fix; ordering only makes the arbitrary choice repeatable. (3) LINES 172-183, class_to_modality(). It reads `brick_classes` and ignores `label_contains` / `label_excludes`, which is where the config resolves exactly these collisions (door vs window contact; room occupancy vs a lift car). Either honour them -- the point's label is already fetched at line 155 and passed to the loop at line 324 -- or, if that is too much, at least make `setdefault` LOUD: warn when a class is claimed by more than one modality, so the YAML-order tie-break is a decision rather than an accident. COST: (1) is about eight lines and cannot make anything worse -- today it would change no point's outcome on bldg1, which is also how it can be landed safely. (3) is maybe thirty lines and wants a re-run of the dry run to compare counts.
Verification: Read from the source, not inferred: line numbers taken from scripts/link_unlinked_sensors.py as of 2026-09-30. class_to_modality() re-run standalone against config/saturation_modalities.yaml: 70 classes mapped; Occupancy_Status -> occupancy_status, Occupancy_Count_Sensor -> occupancy, Motion_Sensor -> occupancy, Contact_Sensor -> door_contact, Open_Close_Status -> door_contact, Availability_Status -> lift_state, Fan_Status -> fan_state. `Status` alone maps to nothing. The six Booking_Status points' full inferred class sets were read from the live graph and contain exactly one mapped class each, which is why no point is affected today. NOT A MEASURED FAILURE -- a latent one, filed as such.

Title: CAVEAT-1115's remaining ~77 passes-on-empty tests: 40 guarded, 63+11 hits down to 32+1, and not one was hiding a product defect
Description: Re-derived both AST sweeps from CAVEAT-1115's description and worked the backlog. Starting state on the current tree: 68 EMPTY-COLLECTION hits had become 63 and 15 FILTERED-LOOP hits had become 11 (the previous agent guarded six). Finishing state: 32 and 1. Every remaining hit was READ and dispositioned rather than left unexplained, and they fall into four kinds the scanner cannot tell apart from the dangerous shape, counted from the finished scan rather than from memory: (a) a loop over range(N), a range-backed generator or a literal the test itself wrote, which cannot be empty -- 9 (backfill, binary_points, forecast_pipeline, policy_engine, potability, wide_sensor_values, generated_readings, the_reach_report, ticket_universe); (b) a loop over ast.walk(tree) whose assertions are actually in a SECOND loop over a literal tuple of banned words -- 3 (comparison_windows, coverage_gap, forecast_scope); (c) a call site whose collection is now guarded inside the HELPER or FIXTURE that produces it, which the scanner cannot see through -- 17, and this is where most of the fixing went, because one assert in _rows / _closures / _modalities / _pairs / _roles / _truth / _refreshed_rows / the plant `spec` fixture covers every caller at once; (d) a test that already carries a sibling non-empty guard, an inline size assert or an explicit pytest.skip -- 3 (av_readiness, config_panel_assets, register_predicates). 9 + 3 + 17 + 3 = 32, which is the total the scan reports. Roughly 40 assertions were added across 39 files. THE HEADLINE IS THE DISAPPOINTING ONE AND IS SAID PLAINLY: strengthening these found ZERO product defects. Four tests went red, and all four were the TEST -- see BUG-1182, CAVEAT-1183, BUG-1184 and the quoting bug in test_meter_boundary where ast.unparse normalises " to ' and silently stops a needle matching its own source.
Root_Cause: lessons #20 one level up: 'couldn't check' and 'checked, found nothing' render identically, and a loop that IS the whole test is a fail-open path with no count of how often it acted. The most useful distinction found while grinding through them: a collection that comes from a LITERAL the test wrote is not this defect, and a blanket guard on one is noise. The ones worth the assert are those whose iterable is produced by the code under test, by a parse of a shipped file, or by a filesystem glob -- because those are the three that can quietly become empty.
Fix_Approach: A size assertion where the iterable must be non-empty; a counter where an in-loop `continue` can filter everything out; an explicit pytest.skip with a reason where zero is LEGITIMATE for one parameter but not for the set (the first-aid records, CAVEAT-1183). Prioritised by what the test guards, not by how easy it was: RBAC and persona separation (test_access_tiers, test_cross_role_consistency, test_acceptance_scenarios), privacy (test_event_and_capacity_provisioning's personal-identifier scan, now counting both filtered arms), secrets (test_every_setting_is_discoverable, floor of 4 because STRICT_SECRETS refuses to boot on four), design contract 3 (test_coverage_audit, test_endpoint_parity_probe, test_bldg4_fixture, test_absent_referent_metrics), fabrication (test_a_question_about_the_conversation..., which now requires the recall answer to quote at least one identifier), and safety (the defibrillator pair). Cosmetic ones were left alone and are listed in the Description as (a)-(d) so the next reader does not re-derive the triage.
Verification: Both scans re-run on the finished tree: EMPTY 63 -> 32, FILTERED 11 -> 1. Targeted pytest over all 39 touched files after black --line-length 100 and flake8 --select=F821,F823 (exit 0). Four tests went red on first strengthening and each was investigated to a root cause before being logged; none was a product defect.
Refs: CAVEAT-1115; CAVEAT-1060; lessons #20-22; lessons #153; BUG-1182; CAVEAT-1183; BUG-1184

Title: The persona/RBAC separation guard read two attributes PersonaRegistry has never had, so it examined zero of twelve personas
Description: tests/test_acceptance_scenarios.py::TestScenario8RoleConsistency::test_personas_carry_no_permissions did `getattr(registry, "personas", None) or getattr(registry, "_personas", {})` and PersonaRegistry exposes NEITHER -- its attributes are `_registry` and `all_personas()`. The chain therefore fell through to `{}` every run and the loop body never executed. Measured: all_personas() returns 12 names on the active building (8 built in, plus auditor, caretaker and facility_manager merged from input/personas/), and the test had checked none of them. This is design contract 5 -- personas bias classification and framing only, never permissions -- and it was unguarded. Repaired and re-run: 12 personas examined, none mentions 'permission', 'rbac' or 'allow_role'. NO PRODUCT DEFECT: the separation holds. The test was the whole of the problem.
Root_Cause: A getattr chain with a `{}` fallback cannot distinguish 'this object does not have that attribute' from 'it has it and it is empty', and the loop that follows renders both as a pass. The fallback was written defensively, against a registry shape that was never measured.
Fix_Approach: Read the registry through its real API -- `all_personas()` for the names, `_registry[name]` for each spec -- and assert the name list is non-empty before looping. A getattr fallback is only safe where the absent case is asserted separately; here it was the only case.
Verification: Before: `getattr(registry, 'personas', '<missing>')` and `_personas` both print '<missing>'. After: pytest tests/test_acceptance_scenarios.py::TestScenario8RoleConsistency -q -> 3 passed, with the log line '[persona_loader] merged personas from disk' confirming the overlay was read.
Refs: CAVEAT-1181; CAVEAT-1115; CLAUDE.md design contract 5; CLAUDE.md design contract 7

Title: Six defibrillator parameters reported PASSED for buildings that declare no first-aid point at all
Description: tests/test_the_defibrillator_record_and_its_answer_agree.py parametrises two tests over every building directory and loops over _first_aid_records(g) with all assertions inside. Counted per directory: input 4, bldg2 1, bldg3 1, and bldg2_source 0, bldg3_source 0, bldg4 0. So six of the nineteen results in that file were passes on a building the test never examined -- exactly the shape CAVEAT-1115 found in test_agent_methods_exist's __init__.py parameter. Where a defibrillator is is not a thing to be quietly not-checking. NO PRODUCT DEFECT: the three buildings that DO declare first-aid points pass on their merits, and the three that do not are a synthetic fixture and two source trees with no amenity records, which is legitimate.
Root_Cause: A parametrised test over a heterogeneous set, where 'this parameter has nothing to check' and 'this parameter checked everything and it was fine' are the same green dot.
Fix_Approach: pytest.skip with the building's name and the reason, so the six say what they are; plus a new test_some_building_declares_a_first_aid_position that sums the counts across all directories and fails at zero. A per-parameter skip alone would let the whole set go quiet together -- one renamed class in _records_graph is enough -- and the file would still report a clean run.
Verification: Before: 19 passed, 0 skipped. After: 14 passed, 6 skipped, each naming its building, plus the new counter test. Counts measured directly through the test module's own helpers rather than inferred from the pass/fail line.

Title: test_outages_never_start_in_the_future sampled 40 lifts at a 0.06 daily rate and generated zero outages, every run
Description: The test builds 40 lift assets, calls outages_for_day for day offsets 0, 1 and 3 against a `now` of 12:00 on day 0, and asserts start_dt <= now inside the loop. Measured: the yield is {0: 0, 1: 0, 3: 0} -- the loop has never run a single assertion. Two things suppress it together. The daily rate for a lift is 0.06, so 40 assets give about 2.4 candidate episodes a day; and `if start > now: continue` removes everything on offsets 1 and 3 outright (their day has not begun) and roughly half of day 0's, since starts fall between 07:00 and 19:00. At 200 assets the yield is {0: 3, 1: 0, 3: 0}, which is the split the test is actually about. NO PRODUCT DEFECT -- the filter is demonstrably the thing suppressing them, not the rate: with `now` at 23:59 on day 0 the same 200 assets yield 15 instead of 3, and day+1 still yields 0.
Root_Cause: A probabilistic generator sampled below its own detection threshold. Nothing in the test expressed how many episodes it needed to see, so the sample size was free to be too small and the test was free to be green about it.
Fix_Approach: 200 assets instead of 40, the per-offset counts kept rather than discarded, and two assertions instead of one: the current day must produce at least one episode (otherwise no start_dt was compared with anything), and the two later days must produce exactly zero (which is the `start > now` filter working, and is the half of the property a positive-only count would miss).
Verification: Yield measured directly at n=40/200/400/1000 before changing anything: totals 0, 3, 8, 26. pytest tests/test_asset_state_lane.py -q -> 54 passed. The first strengthening (a bare non-empty assert at n=40) went RED, which is how this was found; the threshold, not the suspicion, was what needed correcting.

Title: A 2200-character window over a 773-character method: the token it matched was in the next method entirely
Description: CAVEAT-1120's shape, in a file nobody had connected to it. tests/test_configuration_history_wiring.py::TestReachability::test_the_caveat_reuses_the_loaded_history_rather_than_querying_again asserted `"_config_history" in src[src.index("async def _configuration_caveat"):][:2200]`. Measured against the parsed tree: _configuration_caveat is 773 characters, so the window spilled 1427 characters PAST THE END of the method it names, and _config_history does not appear in that method at all -- it is a try/except wrapper around _configuration_caveat_inner, which is where the logic went. The assertion has been passing on its neighbour. The sibling window over _load_configuration_periods spills 303 characters for the same reason, though its needles do sit inside the real function. THE PROPERTY HELD THE WHOLE TIME -- _configuration_caveat_inner does read _config_history and does not call for_building -- so this is a test defect, and the negative half (`assert "for_building" not in body`) is the worrying direction: it was only accidentally complete, and would have gone quiet the moment the inner method grew past the spill.
Root_Cause: A character window is a bet on how much code sits around the anchor, and a refactor that splits a method into a wrapper and an _inner moves the logic without moving the anchor. lessons #151 forbids the form; CAVEAT-1120 predicted this exact consequence for capability_agent and it landed here first.
Fix_Approach: A _method_and_its_helpers(name) helper that parses _orchestrator.py, takes the named method's source via ast.get_source_segment, and follows one level of `self._helper(...)` delegation. The property belongs to the wrapper/_inner PAIR, not to whichever half keeps the name, so following the delegation is what makes the check survive the next refactor rather than merely fixing this one. Verified the helper resolves to the wrapper plus _configuration_caveat_inner and NOT to _recheck_line, which the old window would have started reaching next.
Verification: Function extents measured from the AST: _configuration_caveat 773 chars vs a 2200 window; '_config_history' in the window True, in the whole function FALSE, and present in the spill. After the rewrite: pytest tests/test_configuration_history_wiring.py -q -> 22 passed, and the assembled source is 1970 characters covering exactly the two methods.

Title: xfail_strict = true is now set, and the audit's reason for calling it safe was half wrong
Description: CAVEAT-1113 recommended it and said the three remaining unit xfails already set strict=True. Checked rather than taken on trust, and the count is different: tests/ holds exactly THREE xfail sites, not three unit ones. ONE is inside -m unit (test_event_and_capacity_provisioning.py:172, BUG-695 modelling debt, parametrised into three cases) and it does carry strict=True. The other two -- test_capability_e2e.py:187 and test_non_regression_intents.py:133 -- carry strict=False and sit in files whose module-level pytestmark is pytest.mark.live, so they are outside -m unit entirely. The conclusion 'safe today' survives, but for a different reason than the one given: every existing marker passes `strict` EXPLICITLY, and an explicit kwarg beats the ini default, so the setting is inert for the whole current tree and only changes what a marker written tomorrow does by default.
Root_Cause: n/a -- recorded because the next reader will otherwise inherit the wrong count. A non-strict xfail cannot report that it has started passing (CAVEAT-1113); this makes strict the default so that the next one written without a kwarg fails loudly when its defect is fixed.
Fix_Approach: One line in pytest.ini plus a comment recording what was measured and which three markers exist, so a future reader does not have to re-derive whether it is safe.
Verification: The override was MEASURED, not cited: a throwaway file with one xfail(strict=False) that passes and one xfail with no kwarg that passes, run twice against two ini files. Without the setting: 2 xpassed. With xfail_strict=true: 1 failed (the kwarg-less one) and 1 xpassed (the explicit strict=False one, unchanged). Then on the repo: pytest tests/test_event_and_capacity_provisioning.py -q -rxX -> 35 passed, 3 xfailed, 0 xpassed, identical before and after the ini change; the two live files still collect (28 tests) and were not run.

Title: Negative result: the two reload-detached settings patch sites are genuinely repaired, confirmed by running the reload rather than reading the diff
Description: CAVEAT-1110 reported fixing test_analytics_repairs_inside_a_time_budget.py:129 and test_observed_at.py:114. Confirmed by the technique lesson #159 prescribes, executed rather than reasoned about. The detachment is real and reproduces: `analytics_agent.settings is shared.config.settings` is True before importlib.reload(shared.config) and False after. Both sites now reach the object the product reads -- analytics_agent holds its binding at module level and the test patches _aa.settings, the same attribute lookup; evidence/assemble.py does `from shared.config import settings` INSIDE _as_datetime and the test patches _cfg.settings, which resolves at call time to the same post-reload object. The counterfactual was measured too: the OLD style at each site misses. A fresh `from shared.config import settings` in the analytics test body reaches a DIFFERENT object from the one analytics_agent reads, and a module-level pre-reload binding in test_observed_at would likewise miss what assemble reads.
Root_Cause: n/a -- a verification, recorded so the next session does not re-open it. The point worth keeping: the repairs are load-bearing, not cosmetic, because both counterfactuals come back False.
Fix_Approach: None needed; both sites are correct as they stand.
Verification: BEFORE reload aa.settings is cfg.settings: True. AFTER reload: False. SITE 1 test target is product target: True; old style reaches: False. SITE 2 test target is product target: True; old style reaches: False.

Title: The char-window sweep is 35 sites, not 3, and the one I flagged as the worst was disproved by its own counterfactual
Description: CAVEAT-1114 found three windows and rewrote two. Widening the scan from 'integer slice inside an assert' to 'integer slice of SOURCE TEXT that the assertions read' finds 35: 7 directly inside an assertion's test expression and 28 of the form `block = src[src.index(ANCHOR):][:N]` bound one line above it. They were then ranked by whether they can go false-GREEN rather than merely false-RED, by counting how often each asserted needle occurs in the product file and how far the intended one sits from the anchor. THE TOP-RANKED ONE WAS WRONG AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS SO: test_meter_boundary's `assert "except Exception" in block[:900]` looked alarming (147 occurrences in _orchestrator.py, intended one at +477), so the try it guards was deleted in memory and the window re-checked -- and the next handler falls OUTSIDE 900 characters, so the assertion would have gone red as intended. Not a false pass. CAVEAT-1185 is the one that WAS, and it was ranked lower by the same heuristic, because its needle occurs only twice.
Root_Cause: Occurrence-count heuristics rank the risk of a window, they do not decide it. What decides it is whether the window's extent matches the CONSTRUCT's extent, which needs the parsed tree -- the same answer lesson #151 gives for how to write the assertion in the first place.
Fix_Approach: Three rewritten to read the AST: the two config-history windows via _method_and_its_helpers (CAVEAT-1185), and test_meter_boundary's pair -- 'the boundary never costs the answer' is now a structural question (find the ast.Try whose body calls self._meter_boundary_line, assert its handlers catch Exception) rather than a text search, which is also the question its name asks. One trap worth recording: ast.unparse NORMALISES quoting, so a needle written with double quotes stops matching its own source -- use ast.get_source_segment when the assertion is about text. The remaining 30 are inventoried here rather than rewritten; the scan is a 60-line script and is described precisely enough above to re-derive.
Verification: 35 sites enumerated; 28 window extents measured against the parsed function they anchor to; one counterfactual mutation run in memory to disprove the top-ranked false-green. pytest tests/test_meter_boundary.py -q -> 68 passed; tests/test_configuration_history_wiring.py -q -> 22 passed.

Title: A modality the signal generator does not model is backfilled as a gapless series of the value 0.0, and stored as readings
Description:
`orchestrator/services/deliberation/synthetic_signals.py::modality_series` dispatches on the modality parsed out of `<space>_sat_<modality>` and models twelve: occupancy, co2, door_contact, temperature, humidity, noise, illuminance, window_contact, pm25, energy_submeter, water_flow, parking_free. Every other modality falls to `else:  # unknown modality: neutral zero signal, never invented physics` -> `out.append(0.0)`. `scripts/backfill_saturation.py` then INSERTs that straight into the narrow tables at a 10-minute cadence.
MEASURED IN THE STORE: nitrogen_dioxide, pm10, pm1, formaldehyde, carbon_monoxide and tvoc each hold EXACTLY 30,240 zeros (5,040 per point x 6 points = 5 weeks x 7 x 144 slots), 100.00% on a ten-minute boundary, window 2026-08-12 00:00:00 .. 2026-09-15 23:50:00, with ZERO non-zero rows anywhere inside it. lighting_cct: 471,744 zeros (2,016 per point x 234 = 2 weeks x 7 x 144), 100.00% on the grid, window 2026-09-02 .. 2026-09-15 23:50:00, again no non-zero row inside. 45% of every lighting colour-temperature reading this building holds is 0 K.
Root_Cause: The comment states the intent - 'never invented physics' - and it is exactly backwards once the value reaches a store. 0.0 is not the absence of a reading; it is a reading of zero, and it survives every range check that tests a minimum, poisons every mean, and is indistinguishable downstream from a real measurement. This is the 'four kinds of nothing' lesson one layer lower than it is usually found: absence encoded as a value, in the store rather than in a lane. The generator was right to refuse to invent a shape; it should have refused to write a row.
Fix_Approach:
NOT APPLIED HERE, deliberately, for two reasons that are about this stack rather than about the diagnosis.
(1) `synthetic_signals.py` is LOADED LIVE by the data-publisher from a read-only mount (`_GENERATOR_FILES` in mysql-dummy-publish-dev/mysql_dummy_publisher.py), so editing it changes what is being written to the store right now, and store writes belong to the owner.
(2) `tests/test_synthetic_signals.py::test_unknown_modality_yields_zeros_not_invented_physics` PINS the zero fallback by name. A guard test that fails your fix is doing its job (lesson #153); overruling it is a design decision about what 'no model for this modality' should write, not a bug fix, and it is the owner's.
PROPOSED: `modality_series` returns None (or raises) for an unmodelled modality, and `backfill_saturation._backfill` skips those points and NAMES them in its summary - so a modality nobody has modelled shows up as a gap somebody can see, not as thirty-five days of zero. The test above becomes `test_unknown_modality_writes_nothing_rather_than_zero` and keeps its intent. Existing rows are NOT rewritten: see CAVEAT-1131 on not rewriting history.
URGENCY: the zeros stopped at 2026-09-15 23:50 only because the backfill is a manual script. Nothing prevents the next run from writing more.
Verification:
scratchpad/probe_zero_cadence.py, in-container 2026-09-30 12:23 UTC, MySQL session printed as '+00:00'. Per family: zeros, share on a ten-minute boundary, the window, and the count of NON-zero rows inside that same window. The last of those is the decisive one and it is 0 for every family tested, which is what separates a backfill from an alternating writer. STEP_MINUTES = 10 in synthetic_signals.py; `--weeks 5` and `--weeks 2` reproduce 5,040 and 2,016 exactly.
CONTROL: `_sat_occupancy_status` is NOT this defect - 31.69% of its zeros are on the grid and 1,005,535 non-zero rows share the window, which is what a modelled modality looks like.
Refs: CAVEAT-1132; CAVEAT-1131; CAVEAT-1173; lesson 'four kinds of nothing'; orchestrator/services/deliberation/synthetic_signals.py; scripts/backfill_saturation.py; tests/test_synthetic_signals.py

Title: 256 points declared binary hold 361,272 rows above 1, up to 194 - a booking status of 189.484 and an intrusion detector of 194
Description: Measured 2026-09-30 12:22 UTC. 256 points in occupancy_data carry the band [0,1] (BinaryState, from `brick:Occupancy_Sensor`/`Occupancy_Status`/`Contact_Sensor`), and across 3,136,268 rows they hold 361,272 values above 1 and 369,309 values that are neither 0 nor 1, reaching 194.0. Worst families by violation count: PIR_Lighting_Floor0..5, IntrusionDetector_Floor0..5, Booking_Status_Room1_25/1_26/3_13/3_26/5_15/5_16, EV_Charger_1/2_State_Sensor and Lift_1_Status_Sensor, each 14,700-18,200 rows. Last such row 2026-09-16 14:35:14; zero in the last 24 hours.
Root_Cause: Not diagnosed here. It is the RETRO half of CAVEAT-1131 in its most visible form: these points now carry [0,1] and previously took the occupancy COLUMN's default (0,30), so a state flag was generated as a people count. But the values reach 194, which (0,30) could not produce either, so at least one other writer is involved - most likely the same one behind the 194s in the counter series. Separated from CAVEAT-1132 because the mechanism differs: these are not zeros, they are counts standing where a state belongs.
Fix_Approach: NOT ATTEMPTED. Recorded because a lane that reads a Booking_Status of 189.484 as a boolean will read it as TRUE, and one that averages it will report a booking rate of 18,948%. Nothing here is live, so this is about what a question reaching back over August and early September would return, not about what is being written.
Verification: scratchpad/probe_gases.py, in-container, session printed '+00:00'. Points selected from the publish map by band == [0,1] and table == occupancy_data, so the selection is the building's own declaration rather than a name match.

Title: The band audit is blind to a zero that lies inside its band, and under-counted the backfilled-zero family by a third
Description: `scripts/audit_declared_band_conformance.py` finds values outside [lo, hi]. BUG-1171's zero backfill hit SIX gas families with identical counts - 30,240 zeros each - but the audit reported only FOUR, because carbon_monoxide (band [0,5]) and tvoc (band [0,387]) have a floor of 0, so their zeros are inside the band and invisible to it. CAVEAT-1132 was filed as 'four gases, one shape' on exactly that output, and the shape is six.
Root_Cause: The instrument answers 'is this value outside the range the building declares ordinary?' while the question being asked of it was 'is this value a measurement?'. Those are different sentences, and a band cannot express the second: a sentinel, a zero standing for absence and a genuine zero are all inside [0, 5]. Lesson #160 in a new place - before trusting a metric, say out loud what it counts and what you wanted counted.
Fix_Approach: NOT ATTEMPTED, and widening the band check is the wrong fix - it would flag every legitimate zero. What finds this family is the SHAPE, not the value: a complete, gapless run of one identical value on a fixed grid with no other value anywhere in the window. That is a different audit (a constant-run detector) and would also catch the stuck-sensor case the anomaly scanner exists for. Recorded so the next reader of a band audit knows what it cannot see.
Verification: Measured 2026-09-30: nitrogen_dioxide/pm10/pm1/formaldehyde appear in the band audit with 30,240 violations each; carbon_monoxide and tvoc appear with none, and a direct COUNT of `value = 0` on those two returns 30,240 each over the identical window. scratchpad/probe_gases.py.

Title: Running the checked-in publish-map generator by hand silently strips every band from the map and reinstates BUG-439
Description:
Two things write `input/<id>_narrow_publish_map.json` and they disagree about what belongs in it. `orchestrator/services/publisher_map.py::_rebuild` calls `generate_publisher_map.build_map` and THEN `_attach_bands`, which reads `ontosage:typicalMin/typicalMax` per point from the graph - that is where all 2,511 bands in the live map come from. `scripts/generate_publisher_map.py::main`, run on its own, writes `build_map`'s output DIRECTLY: 2,756 entries with no lo, no hi and no dec. Its own final line says 'Recreate the publisher so it reloads the map', so it presents itself as the way to refresh it.
CONSEQUENCE: the publisher falls back to `_NARROW_RANGES`, keyed by COLUMN. Every gas in this building writes to `iaq_data.voc`, so carbon monoxide would again inherit TVOC's 50-350 and publish at ~204 ppm against a declared ordinary range of 0-5. That is BUG-439/BUG-609's defect, and one hand-run of a script that looks like the right script brings it back.
Root_Cause: The derivation was split across two owners to satisfy `tests/test_a_provisioned_point_is_fed.py::test_the_derivation_has_one_implementation`, which forbids the service from reimplementing the table and value column rule. The band rule then landed in the service because it needs the graph - so the generator has one half of the answer and nothing says so. The test is right about its own property and does not cover this one.
Fix_Approach: NOT ATTEMPTED - it touches a file another agent was asked not to have changed under it this session. Cheapest honest fix, in order of preference: (a) move `_attach_bands` into `generate_publisher_map.py` so one module owns the whole entry, and have the service call it - this satisfies the existing test rather than fighting it; (b) failing that, make `main()` refuse to write a map with no bands unless given an explicit flag, and say why. Either is small. Leaving it is the expensive option, because the failure is silent, looks like a successful refresh, and reintroduces a P1-class fabrication.
Verification: Read from source 2026-09-30: `generate_publisher_map.build_map` returns entries with keys uuid/table/value_col/label/sensor only, and `main()` writes `json.dumps(entries)` with nothing in between. `publisher_map._rebuild` calls `_attach_bands(points)` after it. The live map carries lo/hi on 2,511 of 2,756 entries; `git show a45bf47:bldg1/bldg1_narrow_publish_map.json` - written before the service existed - carries them on 0 of 1,738, which is what a generator-only map looks like.
Refs: BUG-439; BUG-609; CAVEAT-1131; BUG-1135; scripts/generate_publisher_map.py; orchestrator/services/publisher_map.py

Title: Orchestrator ran away to 40 GiB and 3210% CPU, stopped serving, and Docker still reported healthy
Description:
MEASURED on the live container while it was unresponsive:
    CPU      3210.31%   (32 cores pegged)
    MEMORY   40.02 GiB of 46.64 GiB  (86% of the machine)
    health   'healthy' -- with FAILING STREAK 2 and last check 12:47:01, an hour stale
After `docker compose restart orchestrator`: **1.326 GiB and 6.43% CPU**. A 30x memory difference on the same build doing nothing.
SYMPTOMS IT PRODUCED, in order: the last log line was 12:49:34 and then NOTHING for an hour -- not even the ECA rules engine, which had been logging a MySQL query every ~10 s continuously. `/health` timed out at 20 s. `/auth/login` timed out at 30 s, so the live re-ask batch could not authenticate and exited. `Login Postgres probe failed: TimeoutError` at 12:48:05 was the first visible sign, and it reads as a Postgres fault, which it is not -- Postgres was up, healthy, and using 41.93 MiB.
**THE OPERATIONAL POINT IS THE HEALTHCHECK.** `docker ps` said `Up 3 hours (healthy)` throughout. The status was frozen from before the runaway because the check itself had stopped completing, and a stale PASS is indistinguishable from a fresh one in `docker ps`. Anyone triaging this from `docker ps` alone would have ruled the orchestrator out first.
Root_Cause:
NOT DIAGNOSED. What is established is the runaway itself and that a restart clears it; what consumed 40 GiB is not established, and a heap profile of a wedged 40 GiB process was not practical to take.
THE STRONGEST CANDIDATE, on evidence gathered before the wedge: the deliberation lane. BUG-1192 measured ONE `coverage_audit` step enumerating **39,119 located points in 13m15s** inside a single turn, and CAVEAT-1193 established that abandoned turns keep running after their client leaves -- one ran ~16 minutes past its harness's timeout. Several such turns overlapping is a plausible way to accumulate that much resident memory. PLAUSIBLE, NOT SHOWN.
WHAT THIS PROBABLY EXPLAINS, and each needs re-testing against a healthy process rather than being assumed closed:
  * BUG-1191 -- `asyncio.wait_for(180 s)` not firing on a 3,239 s call. An     event loop on a process at 3210% CPU and 86% memory may simply not be     reaching its timer callbacks. That is a far more economical explanation     than an Ollama-side stall, and it means the LLM was probably never the     problem.
  * CAVEAT-942, both instances (3,102 s and 3,412 s).
  * The gate's progressive slowdown: the same 51 cases ran median 30.3 s /     27.8 min total at 08:52, and 1h40m to reach case 9 that afternoon.
TIMING CAVEAT I WILL NOT PAPER OVER: the 40 GiB was measured AFTER an hour of wedge. Memory during case 8 (11:06) was not sampled, so 'the runaway caused the 54-minute call' is a hypothesis about an earlier moment I have no measurement for. The right next step is to sample container memory ALONGSIDE the gate, which costs one background `docker stats` loop.
Fix_Approach:
1. INSTRUMENT FIRST, because this has now cost a day of misattribution: run `docker stats` into a log for the duration of any gate or probe run, so latency figures can be read against memory. Cheap, and it decides BUG-1191.
2. Make the healthcheck able to FAIL. A check that stops completing must not leave a frozen `healthy`; a shorter interval with a low retry count, and an explicit memory ceiling on the service, would have surfaced this in minutes rather than an hour.
3. Bound the deliberation lane (BUG-1192) and give the workflow a deadline that abandons its own work (CAVEAT-1193). Those are the two mechanisms most likely to be feeding the growth.
NOT ATTEMPTED TODAY: any of it. A memory ceiling that OOM-kills the orchestrator mid-measurement would trade a slow failure for an abrupt one before the cause is known.
=== CONTROLS BUILT AND MEASURED 2026-09-30 (orchestrator recreated at 14:17:10Z) ===
Point 1 of the plan above is DONE, 2 is DONE, 3 is NOT. The runaway itself is STILL NOT DIAGNOSED and this row stays open on that -- what follows bounds the harm and makes the next occurrence diagnosable; it does not explain the first one.

1. A HEALTHCHECK THAT CAN FAIL. All four compose files (`docker-compose.yml` + bldg2/bldg3/bldgtest), identically:
       test: ["CMD","curl","-fsS","--max-time","8","http://localhost:8000/ping"]
       interval: 15s   timeout: 10s   retries: 3   start_period: 360s (UNCHANGED)
   `--max-time` is the part that matters. Docker's own `timeout:` only helps if the daemon can REAP a hung exec, and on the day it could not -- FailingStreak stuck at 2 with no further entries. curl exiting 28 on its own is a failure the health monitor records without needing to kill anything. `timeout: 10s` is deliberately LONGER than `--max-time 8` so curl always loses the race to itself.
   start_period stays at 360s on purpose: shortening it re-opens BUG-246, a false `(unhealthy)` on every single boot, which is how people are trained to ignore health flags.

2. A MEMORY CEILING, HARD, AND THE TRADE IS STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED.
   `mem_limit: ${ORCHESTRATOR_MEM_LIMIT:-8g}` with `memswap_limit` equal to it, so swap is OFF for this container. 8 GiB is four times the 2.01 GiB ceiling measured under a full 51-case gate load.
   WHY HARD AND NOT AN ALARM: an alarm needs a reader, and the failure being fixed is that nobody knew for an hour while the one automated watcher had frozen. More decisively -- the runaway starved the HOST (86% of 46.64 GiB), and that is what stopped the probe from running at all. A cgroup limit confines the blast radius to one container BY CONSTRUCTION. No alarm can do that, however loud.
   WHAT IT COSTS, and it is a real cost, not a free win: an OOM kill ends every in-flight turn abruptly -- a reset connection, no answer, and exit 137 as the only explanation -- and `restart: unless-stopped` then costs a cold start measured today at 3m27s (14:17:10Z -> /health 200 at 14:20:37Z) during which nothing is served at all. A gate, probe or tail-N run that straddles a kill is lost and must be re-run. Against an hour of a wedged process that loses the same turns, reports `healthy`, and misdirects triage at the same time, the trade is worth taking. But it does mean a measurement can now be destroyed in one second instead of degraded over an hour, and whoever is running one should know that.
   RESIDUAL RISK, MEASURED not assumed: `restart: unless-stopped` plus a DETERMINISTIC OOM is a crash loop. A throwaway container at --memory=256m with an allocating loop restarted 7 times in ~40 s, docker backing off 1s, 1s, 2s, 4s between them. This runaway is not deterministic at boot -- the process idles at 1.20 GiB -- so a loop is not expected. The check is `docker inspect --format '{{.RestartCount}}/{{.State.OOMKilled}}'`, and unlike the health status it cannot go stale.
   NOT DONE, deliberately: no limit on any other service. graphdb sits at 2.4 GiB and redis at 0.87 GiB and neither has ever run away. One limit, on the one container that did.

3. NOT DONE: bounding the deliberation lane (BUG-1192) or giving the workflow a deadline that abandons its own work (CAVEAT-1193). Both stay open. The measurements below are why they were not touched: on a healthy process the lane is FAST, so a bound sized from the incident's numbers would have been sized from a symptom.

4. INSTRUMENTATION -- `orchestrator/services/process_watchdog.py`, started from `main.lifespan`, stopped on shutdown.
   Every 30 s at INFO: cgroup memory computed the way `docker stats` computes it (usage minus inactive_file), `anon`, peak, delta since the last sample, the share of the limit, EVENT-LOOP LAG and the thread count. WARNING above 60% of the limit (or 6 GiB when unlimited), or when the loop has not ticked for 30 s.
   IT RUNS IN AN OS THREAD, NOT ON THE LOOP. The failure it instruments is one where asyncio timers demonstrably did not fire, so an `asyncio.sleep` loop would have gone quiet at exactly the moment it was needed. A one-second heartbeat task stamps a monotonic clock and the thread reports how stale it is, which is the direct positive evidence for 'the loop never reached its timer callbacks' that nobody had.
   THE SECOND-ORDER WIN IS THE ONE TO REMEMBER. During the incident the logs went silent for an hour and that silence was AMBIGUOUS -- idle and wedged render identically. With a 30 s heartbeat line, `docker logs --since 2m ontosage-orchestrator | grep watchdog` returning NOTHING is now a positive wedge test that needs no exec, no /health, and no healthcheck, and therefore cannot be defeated by the thing that defeated all three.
   Env: WATCHDOG_ENABLED / WATCHDOG_INTERVAL_S / WATCHDOG_MEM_WARN_GIB / WATCHDOG_LOOP_LAG_WARN_S, all documented in `.env.example`.
Tests: tests/test_orchestrator_healthcheck_can_fail.py (24 cases, bounds not equalities, so tightening further cannot fail them), tests/test_process_watchdog.py (16).
